Floer Simple Manifolds and L-Space IntervalsThanks: JR was partially supported by EPSRC grant EP/M000648/1Thanks: SDR was supported by EPSRC grant EP/M000648/1

Jacob Rasmussen Address: Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics, University of Cambridge, UK Email address: J.Rasmussen@dpmms.cam.ac.uk and Sarah Dean Rasmussen Address: Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics, University of Cambridge, UK Email address: S.Rasmussen@dpmms.cam.ac.uk
Abstract.

An oriented three-manifold with torus boundary admits either no L-space Dehn filling, a unique L-space filling, or an interval of L-space fillings. In the latter case, which we call “Floer simple,” we construct an invariant which computes the interval of L-space filling slopes from the Turaev torsion and a given slope from the interval’s interior. As applications, we give a new proof of the classification of Seifert fibered L-spaces over S2S^{2}\!, and prove a special case of a conjecture of Boyer and Clay [6] about L-spaces formed by gluing three-manifolds along a torus.

1. Introduction

An oriented rational homology 3-sphere YY is called an L-space if the Heegaard Floer homology H​F^​(Y){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y) satisfies H​F^​(Y,𝔰)≃ℤ{{\widehat{HF}}}(Y,\mathfrak{s})\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}} for each Spinc{{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}} structure 𝔰\mathfrak{s} on YY. Recent interest in the topological meaning of this condition has been stirred by a conjecture of Boyer, Gordon, and Watson [7], which states that a prime oriented three-manifold YY is an L-space if and only if π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is non left-orderable. Subsequently, Boyer and Clay [6] studied a relative version of this problem for manifolds with toroidal boundary.

In this paper, we study the set of L-space fillings of a connected manifold YY with a single torus boundary component. If YY is such a manifold, we let

Sl(Y)={α∈H1(∂Y)|αis primitive}/±1Sl(Y)=\{\alpha\in H_{1}(\partial Y)\,|\,\alpha\ \text{is primitive}\}/\pm 1

be the set of slopes on ∂Y\partial Y. S​l​(Y)Sl(Y) is a one-dimensional projective space defined over the rational numbers. If we fix a basis ⟨μ,λ⟩\langle\mu,\lambda\rangle for H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y), we can identify S​l​(Y)Sl(Y) with ℚ¯:=ℚ∪{∞}\overline{{{\mathbb{Q}}}}:={{\mathbb{Q}}}\cup\{\infty\} via the map a​μ+b​λ↦a/ba\mu+b\lambda\mapsto a/b. We denote by Y⁡(α)Y(\alpha) the closed manifold obtained by Dehn filling YY with slope α\alpha, and let Kα⊂Y⁡(α)K_{\alpha}\subset Y(\alpha) be the core of the filling solid torus.

Definition 1.1.

If YY is a compact connected oriented three-manifold with torus boundary,

ℒ⁡(Y)={α∈S​l​(Y)|Y⁡(α)​is an L-space}\mathcal{L}(Y)=\{\alpha\in Sl(Y)\,|\,Y(\alpha)\ \text{is an L-space}\}

is the set of L-space filling slopes of YY.

For the set ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) to be nonempty, we must have b1​(Y)=1b_{1}(Y)=1, which implies that YY is a rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}. In this paper, we will restrict our attention to manifolds with multiple L-space fillings: that is, for which |ℒ⁡(Y)|>1|\mathcal{L}(Y)|>1. Such manifolds can be easily characterized in terms of their Floer homology. Recall that a knot KK in a rational homology sphere Y¯\overline{Y} is Floer simple [20] if the knot Floer homology H​F​K^​(K)≃ℤ|H1​(Y)|\widehat{HFK}(K)\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}}^{|H_{1}(Y)|}. Equivalently, KK is Floer simple if Y¯\overline{Y} is an L-space and the spectral sequence from H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) to H​F^​(Y¯){{\widehat{HF}}}(\overline{Y}) degenerates.

Definition 1.2.

A compact oriented three-manifold YY with torus boundary is Floer simple if it has some Dehn filling Y⁡(α)Y(\alpha) whose core KαK_{\alpha} is a Floer simple knot in Y⁡(α)Y(\alpha).

Then we have

Proposition 1.3.

|ℒ⁡(Y)|>1|\mathcal{L}(Y)|>1 if and only if YY\! is Floer simple.

If Kα⊂Y⁡(α)K_{\alpha}\subset Y(\alpha) is Floer simple, then the Floer homology of any surgery on KαK_{\alpha} can be determined from H​F​K^​(Kα)\widehat{HFK}(K_{\alpha}) using the Ozsváth-Szabó mapping cone. The knot Floer homology, in turn, is determined by the Turaev torsion τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) via the relation

χ⁡(H​F​K^​(Kα))∼(1−[α])​τ​(Y)\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K_{\alpha}))\sim(1-[\alpha])\tau(Y)

established in Proposition 2.1. It follows that if YY is Floer simple, then the Floer homology of any Dehn filling of YY can be determined from the Turaev torsion together with a single α∈ℒ⁡(Y)\alpha\in\mathcal{L}(Y). In particular, we can determine ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) from this data, as described below.

Write H1​(Y)=ℤ⊕TH_{1}(Y)={{\mathbb{Z}}}\oplus T, where TT is a torsion group, and let ϕ:H1​(Y)→ℤ\phi:H_{1}(Y)\to{{\mathbb{Z}}} be the projection. Properly normalized, τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) can be written as a sum

τ⁡(Y)=∑h∈H1​(Y)ϕ⁡(h)≥0ah​[h],\tau(Y)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\in H_{1}(Y)\\ \phi(h)\geq 0\end{subarray}}a_{h}[h],

where ah=1a_{h}=1 for all but finitely many h∈H1​(Y)h\in H_{1}(Y) with ϕ⁡(h)>0\phi(h)>0, and a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0. For example, if H1​(Y)=ℤH_{1}(Y)={{\mathbb{Z}}}, then

τ⁡(Y)=Δ⁡(Y)1−t∈ℤ⁡[[t]],\tau(Y)=\frac{\Delta(Y)}{1-t}\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}[[t]],

where the Alexander polynomial Δ⁡(Y)\Delta(Y) is normalized to be an element of ℤ⁡[t]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[t] and we expand the denominator as a Laurent series in positive powers of tt.

Proposition 1.4.

When YY is Floer simple, every coefficient aha_{h} of τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) is either 00 or 11.

Let S⁡[τ⁡(Y)]={h∈H1​(Y)|ah≠0}S[\tau(Y)]=\{h\in H_{1}(Y)\,|\,a_{h}\neq 0\} denote the support of τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y), and let ι:H1​(∂Y)→H1​(Y)\iota:H_{1}(\partial Y)\to H_{1}(Y) be the map induced by inclusion.

If YY is a Floer simple manifold, we define

𝒟τ(Y)={x−y|x∉S[τ(Y)],y∈S[τ(Y)],ϕ(x)≥ϕ(y)}∩imι⊂H1(Y),{{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}(Y)=\{x-y\,|\,x\notin S[\tau(Y)],y\in S[\tau(Y)],\phi(x)\geq\phi(y)\}\cap\mathrm{im}\,\iota\subset H_{1}(Y),

and write 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y){{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y) for the subset of 𝒟τ​(Y){{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}(Y) consisting of those elements with ϕ⁡(h)>0\phi(h)>0.

Let [l]∈S​l​(Y)[l]\in Sl(Y) be the homological longitude (i.e. ll is a primitive element of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y) such that ι⁡(l)\iota(l) is torsion.) We can now state our first main theorem:

Theorem 1.6.

If YY is Floer simple, then either 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y)=∅{{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y)=\emptyset and ℒ⁡(Y)=S​l​(Y)∖[l]\mathcal{L}(Y)=Sl(Y)\setminus[l], or 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y)≠∅{{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y)\neq\emptyset and ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) is a closed interval whose endpoints are consecutive elements of ι−1(𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y))\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y)).

Given τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) and a Floer simple filling slope α\alpha for YY, it is thus straightforward to determine ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y): the torsion determines the set 𝒟τ​(Y){{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}(Y), and ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) is the smallest interval with endpoints in ι−1(𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y))\iota^{-1}({{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y)) which contains α\alpha in its interior.

1.1. Splicing

Theorem 1.6 can be used to address a problem raised by Boyer and Clay in [6]. Suppose that Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are rational homology solid tori, and that φ:∂Y1→∂Y2\varphi:\partial Y_{1}\to\partial Y_{2} is an orientation reversing diffeomorphism. The manifold Yφ=Y1∪φY2Y_{\varphi}=Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}Y_{2} is said to obtained by splicing Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} together by φ\varphi.

In [6], Boyer and Clay studied how the presence of structure (∗)(*) on Dehn fillings of the pieces Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} relates to the presence of structure (∗)(*) on the splice YφY_{\varphi}, where structure (∗)(*) could be one of three things: 1) a coorientable taut foliation; 2) a left-ordering on π1​(Yφ)\pi_{1}(Y_{\varphi}); or 3) a nontrivial class in H​Fr​e​d​(Yφ)HF^{red}(Y_{\varphi}) (as H​Fr​e​dHF^{red} vanishes on, and only on, L-spaces). When Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are graph manifolds, they obtained very strong results in cases 1) and 2), in addition to less complete results in the third case. The analogy with the first two cases suggests the following conjecture, which is implicit in the work of Boyer and Clay and stated explicitly in certain cases by Hanselman [16].

Conjecture 1.7.

Suppose that Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} as above are boundary incompressible, and let ℒi∘\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{i} be the interior of ℒ⁡(Yi)⊂S​l​(Yi)\mathcal{L}(Y_{i})\subset Sl(Y_{i}). Then YφY_{\varphi} is an L-space if and only if φ∗​(ℒ1∘)∪ℒ2∘=S​l​(Y2)\varphi_{*}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{1})\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{2}=Sl(Y_{2}).

In particular, the conjecture says that in order for YφY_{\varphi} to be an L-space, both Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} must be Floer simple. Our second main result is

Theorem 1.8.

Suppose that Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} as above are Floer simple and have 𝒟τ≠∅{{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}\neq\emptyset, and that φ∗​(ℒ1∘)∪ℒ2∘≠∅\varphi_{*}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{1})\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{2}\neq\emptyset. Then YφY_{\varphi} is an L-space if and only if φ∗​(ℒ1∘)∪ℒ2∘=S​l​(Y2)\varphi_{*}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{1})\cup\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{2}=Sl(Y_{2}).

Hanselman and Watson [19] have proved a similar theorem using bordered Floer homology. The restriction that φ∗​(ℒ1∘)∩ℒ2∘≠∅\varphi_{*}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{1})\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{2}\neq\emptyset represents a limitation of our approach, rather than anything intrinsic to the problem. To be specific, Theorem 1.8 is proved by writing YφY_{\varphi} as surgery on a connected sum of Floer simple knots. When φ∗​(ℒ1∘)∩ℒ2∘=∅\varphi_{*}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{1})\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{2}=\emptyset, we have no convenient way of representing the splice as surgery on a knot in an L-space. In contrast, Hanselman and Watson’s approach does not require this hypothesis, but does need a condition on the bordered Floer homology, which they call simple loop type. In a subsequent joint paper [17], it is shown that the conditions of being Floer simple and being simple loop type are equivalent thus enabling us to remove the hypothesis that φ∗​(ℒ1∘)∩ℒ2∘≠∅\varphi_{*}(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{1})\cap\mathcal{L}^{\circ}_{2}\neq\emptyset. The proof of this fact relies on Proposition 3.9 of the current paper, where we explicitly compute the bordered Floer homology C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) of a Floer simple manifold YY for an appropriate choice of μ,λ∈H1​(∂Y)\mu,\lambda\in H_{1}(\partial Y) parametrizing ∂Y\partial Y.

We briefly discuss those aspects of Conjecture 1.7 which are not covered by Theorem 1.8 and its generalizations. As stated, the conjecture implies that a Floer simple manifold YY with 𝒟τ​(Y)=∅{{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}(Y)=\emptyset is boundary compressible. This is easily seen to be the case when H1​(Y)≃ℤH_{1}(Y)\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}}, or more generally, when YY is semi-primitive (c.f. Proposition 1.9 below), but in general we have very little idea how to address this question. (Indeed, this seems like the weakest point of the conjecture.) The other situation which is not addressed by Theorem 1.8 is the case where one or both of Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} is not Floer simple. It seems plausible that bordered Floer homology could be used to prove the conjecture when |ℒ⁡(Y1)|=1|\mathcal{L}(Y_{1})|=1 and |ℒ⁡(Y2)|>1|\mathcal{L}(Y_{2})|>1, or when |ℒ⁡(Y1)|=|ℒ⁡(Y2)|=1|\mathcal{L}(Y_{1})|=|\mathcal{L}(Y_{2})|=1. In contrast, the case where one or both of the YiY_{i} has no L-space fillings seems considerably more difficult to address with current technology.

1.2. Floer homology solid tori

The class of Floer simple manifolds with 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ=∅{{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}=\emptyset is of special interest. If YY is a rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}, we say that YY is semi-primitive if the torsion subgroup of YY is contained in the image of ι\iota, and that YY has genus 00 if H2​(Y,∂Y)H_{2}(Y,\partial Y) is generated by a surface of genus 00.

Proposition 1.9.

If YY is semi-primitive, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    YY is Floer simple and 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y)=∅{{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y)=\emptyset.

  2. (2)

    YY is Floer simple and has genus 00.

  3. (3)

    YY has genus 00 and has an L-space filling.

For example, if K⊂S1×S2K\subset S^{1}\times S^{2} has a lens space surgery, then the complement of KK satisfies the conditions of the proposition. Such knots have been studied by Berge [3], Gabai [15], Cebanu [10], and Buck, Baker and Leucona [2]. Other examples of such manifolds are discussed in section 7.3.

The conditions of Proposition 1.9 are closely related to Watson’s notion of a Floer homology solid torus. Suppose that YY is a rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} with homological longitude ll, and that m∈H1​(∂Y)m\in H_{1}(\partial Y) satisfies m⋅l=1m\cdot l=1.

Definition 1.10.

[18] YY is a Floer homology solid torus if C​F​D^​(Y,m,l)≃C​F​D^​(Y,m+l,l)\widehat{CFD}(Y,m,l)\simeq\widehat{CFD}(Y,m+l,l).

Proposition 1.11.

If YY satisfies the conditions of Proposition 1.9, then it is a Floer homology solid torus.

Manifolds with 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ(Y)=∅{{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}(Y)=\emptyset play an important role in the notion of NLS detection introduced by Boyer and Clay in [6]. If YY is a rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} and α∈S​l​(Y)\alpha\in Sl(Y), α\alpha is said to be strongly NLS detected if Y⁡(α)Y(\alpha) is not an L-space; α\alpha is NLS detected if certain splicings of YY with a family of Floer homology solid tori are not L-spaces. (For the precise definition, see section 7.2). By Theorem 1.6, the set of strongly NLS detected slopes is either a single point, an open interval in S​l​(Y)Sl(Y), or all of S​l​(Y)Sl(Y). By combining Theorem 1.8 with some direct geometric computation, we can show

Corollary 1.12.

If YY is a rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}, the set of NLS detected slopes in S​l​(Y)Sl(Y) is the closure of the set of strongly NLS detected slopes.

1.3. Seifert fibred spaces

One of the key motivating examples for the conjecture of [7] is the class of Seifert-fibred spaces. Indeed, building on work of Ozsváth, Szabó, Matić, Naimi, Jankins, Neumann, Eisenbud, and Hirsch [38, 31, 33, 24, 11], Lisca and Stipsicz proved

Theorem 1.13.

[32] A Seifert fibred space over S2S^{2} is an L-space if and only it does not admit a coorientable taut foliation.

In combination with a result of Boyer, Rolfsen, and Wiest [8], this also implies that a Seifert-fibred space over S2S^{2} has non left-orderable π1\pi_{1} if and only if it is an L-space. The set of Seifert fibred spaces over S2S^{2} which admit a coorientable taut foliation was explicitly described by Jankins and Neumann [24] and Naimi [33], building on a result of Eisenbud, Hirsch, and Neumann [11].

Any Seifert-fibred space over S2S^{2} can be obtained by Dehn filling a Seifert fibred space over D2D^{2}. It follows easily from work of Ozsváth and Szabó [37] that any Seifert fibred space over D2D^{2} is Floer simple, so we can compute the set of L-space filling slopes using Theorem 1.6. The resulting description of the set of Seifert fibred spaces which are not L-spaces agrees with the Jankins-Neumann set, thus giving a new direct proof of Theorem 1.13.

1.4. Discussion

We conclude with some questions about about Floer simple manifolds and their relation to the conjecture of Boyer, Gordon, and Watson. First, we recall the statement of the conjecture.

Conjecture 1.14.

[7] If YY is a oriented, closed, prime three-manifold, then YY is an L-space if and only if π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is non left-orderable.

A potentially more tractable subset of this problem, raised by Boyer and Clay [6] is:

Question 1.

Suppose YY is Floer simple. Is π1​(Y​(α))\pi_{1}(Y(\alpha)) non left-orderable equivalent to α\alpha being an element of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y)?

The characterization of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) given in Theorem 1.6 should make it possible to conduct more detailed tests of Conjecture 1.14. Since there is already considerable experimental evidence in support of the conjecture, we should also consider what circumstances might explain a positive answer to Question 1. One possible explanation is that the condition of being Floer simple is correlated with some strong geometrical property, which in turn can be related to orderings of π1\pi_{1}.

Question 2.

Is there a geometric characterization of Floer simple manifolds which can be stated without reference to Floer homology?

More generally, we think that Floer simple manifolds are a natural class of manifolds whose geometrical properties should be investigated for their own sake. Some evidence in support of this idea is provided by the frequency of Floer simple manifolds among geometrically simple 3-manifolds (as measured by the SnapPea census). Proposition 1.3 may lead readers familiar with the example of L-space knots in S3S^{3} to suspect that the class of Floer simple manifolds is relatively small, but this is not the case. Of the 59,068 rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}’s in the SnapPy census of manifolds triangulated by at most 9 ideal tetrahedra, nearly 20%20\% have multiple finite fillings, and are thus certifiably Floer simple. Moreover, more than two-thirds of the remaining manifolds have Turaev torsion compatible with their being Floer simple. It seems likely that many of these manifolds are Floer simple as well. (The authors thank Tom Brown for sharing these statistics with them.) For those who like other geometries, we note that every Seifert fibred rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} is Floer simple.

It would be interesting to know what happens to the density of Floer simple manifolds as the complexity increases. Perhaps the most basic question we could ask along these lines is

Question 3.

Are there infinitely many irreducible Floer simple manifolds with the same Turaev torsion?

1.5. Organization

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we review some facts about knot Floer homology and the Ozsváth-Szabó mapping cone. These are used in section 3 to prove Proposition 1.3 and to give a characterization of when a given surgery on a Floer simple knot produces an L-space. In this section, we also explain how to compute the bordered Floer homology of a Floer simple manifold. Theorem 1.6 is proved in In Section 4. In Section 5 we apply Theorem 1.6 to Seifert fibred spaces, thus giving a new proof of Theorem 1.13. The proof of Theorem 1.8 is given in Section 6. Finally, in Section 7, we discuss manifolds with 𝒟[-7]>​[-4]0τ=∅{{\mathcal{D}_{\mkern-11.2mu\phantom{a}{}^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\smaller$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-6]$>$}}{\mbox{\larger[-7]$>$}}\mkern 0.3mu\mathchoice{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\mbox{\smaller$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-3]$0$}}{\raisebox{-0.7pt}{\larger[-4]$0$}}}\!}^{\tau}}}=\emptyset.

2. Knot Floer homology and the Ozsváth-Szabó mapping cone

In this section, we briefly recall some facts about knot Floer homology [36, 43, 40] which will be used in what follows. First, let us fix some notation. Throughout this section, we assume that K⊂Y¯K\subset\overline{Y} is an oriented knot in a rational homology sphere. We let Y=Y¯∖ν⁡(K)Y=\overline{Y}\setminus\nu(K) be its complement, and denote by μ∈H1​(∂Y)\mu\in H_{1}(\partial Y) the class of its meridian. Furthermore, we let T⊂H1​(Y)T\subset H_{1}(Y) be the torsion subgroup, and denote by ϕ:H1​(Y)→ℤ\phi:H_{1}(Y)\to{{\mathbb{Z}}} the projection from H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y) to H1​(Y)/T≃ℤH_{1}(Y)/T\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}}, where the isomorphism is chosen so that ϕ⁡(μ)>0\phi(\mu)>0.

2.1. Knot Floer homology

The knot Floer homology H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is a finitely generated abelian group with an absolute ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading. It decomposes as a direct sum H​F​K^​(K)=⊕H​F​K^​(K,𝔰)\widehat{HFK}(K)=\oplus\widehat{HFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}), where 𝔰\mathfrak{s} runs over the set Spinc​(Y,∂Y){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) of relative Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} structures on (Y,∂Y)(Y,\partial Y). Spinc​(Y,∂Y){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) is an affine copy of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y) (aka H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y) torsor); it has a free transitive action of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y). The group H​F​K^​(K,𝔰)\widehat{HFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}) is trivial for all but finitely many 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y,∂Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y).

Given 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y,∂Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y), we consider the formal sum

χ𝔰​(H​F​K^​(K)):=∑h∈H1​(Y)χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰+h))​[h],\chi_{\mathfrak{s}}(\widehat{HFK}(K)):=\sum_{h\in H_{1}(Y)}\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}+h))[h],

where χ​(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\mathfrak{s})) is defined using the absolute ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading. We view χ𝔰​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi_{\mathfrak{s}}(\widehat{HFK}(K)) as an element of the group ring ℤ​[H1​(Y)]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)]; it is known as the graded Euler characteristic of H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K). Clearly

χ𝔰′​(H​F​K^​(K))=[𝔰−𝔰′]​χ𝔰​(H​F​K^​(K)).\chi_{\mathfrak{s}^{\prime}}(\widehat{HFK}(K))=[\mathfrak{s}-\mathfrak{s}^{\prime}]\chi_{\mathfrak{s}}(\widehat{HFK}(K)).

From now on, we will drop 𝔰\mathfrak{s} from the notation and view χ​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K)) as an element of ℤ​[H1​(Y)]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)], well defined up to global multiplication by elements of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y). We write x∼yx\sim y if x,y∈ℤ⁡[H1​(Y)]x,y\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)] satisfy x=[h]​yx=[h]y for some h∈H1​(Y)h\in H_{1}(Y).

For knots in S3S^{3}, it is well-known that χ​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K)) is the Alexander polynomial of KK. More generally, we have

Proposition 2.1.

χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K))∼(1−[μ])​τ​(Y),\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K))\sim(1-[\mu])\tau(Y), where τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) is the Turaev torsion of YY.

Proof.

H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) can be identified with the sutured Floer homology S​F​H​(Y,γμ)SFH(Y,\gamma_{\mu}) [25], where the suture γμ\gamma_{\mu} consists of two parallel copies of μ\mu. The Euler characteristic of the sutured Floer homology can be described as an appropriately formulated torsion [13]. When ∂Y\partial Y is toroidal, this torsion can be expressed in terms of the Turaev torsion, as in Lemma 6.3 of [13]. (This lemma was stated for links in S3S^{3}, but the proof carries through unchanged.) ∎

A priori, τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) is an element of the field Q​(H1​(Y))Q(H_{1}(Y)) obtained by inverting all elements of ℤ​[H1​(Y)]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)] which are not zero divisors. Choose any primitive μ∈H1​(∂Y)\mu\in H_{1}(\partial Y) with ϕ⁡(μ)≠0\phi(\mu)\neq 0; then 1−[μ]1-[\mu] will not be a zero divisor in ℤ​[H1​(Y)]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)]. It follows from the proposition that τ⁡(Y)∈ℤ⁡[H1​(Y)]​[(1−[μ])−1]⊂Q⁡(H1​(Y))\tau(Y)\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)][(1-[\mu])^{-1}]\subset Q(H_{1}(Y)).

Writing (1−[μ])−1=∑i=0∞[μ]i(1-[\mu])^{-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\,[\mu]^{i} allows us to embed ℤ⁡[H1​(Y)]​[(1−[μ])−1]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[H_{1}(Y)][(1-[\mu])^{-1}] in the Novikov ring

Λϕ[H1(Y)]={∑h∈H1​(Y)ah[h]|#{h|ah≠0,ϕ(h)<k}<∞for allk}.\Lambda_{\phi}[H_{1}(Y)]=\Big\{\sum_{h\in H_{1}(Y)}a_{h}[h]\ \Big|\ \#\{h\,|\,a_{h}\neq 0,\phi(h)<k\}<\infty\ \text{for all}\ k\Big\}.

We will view τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) as an element of Λϕ​[H1​(Y)]\Lambda_{\phi}[H_{1}(Y)]. By choosing a splitting H1​(Y)≃ℤ⊕TH_{1}(Y)\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}}\oplus T, we can identify Λϕ​[H1​(Y)]\Lambda_{\phi}[H_{1}(Y)] with the Laurent series ring ℤ[t−1,t]]⊗ℤ[T]{{\mathbb{Z}}}[t^{-1},t]]\otimes{{\mathbb{Z}}}[T], which we shall later sometimes call the “Laurent series group ring.”

As an element of the Novikov ring, τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) is well-defined up to multiplication by elements of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y). We shall always normalize so that τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) has the form τ⁡(Y)=∑hah​[h]\tau(Y)=\sum_{h}a_{h}[h], where ah=0a_{h}=0 for all hh with ϕ⁡(h)<0\phi(h)<0, and a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0.

If H1​(Y)=ℤH_{1}(Y)={{\mathbb{Z}}}, it is well-known that τ⁡(Y)∼Δ⁡(Y)/(1−t)\tau(Y)\sim\Delta(Y)/(1-t), where Δ⁡(Y)\Delta(Y) is the Alexander polynomial of YY. More generally, if Φ:Λϕ[H1(Y)]→ℤ[t−1,t]]\Phi:\Lambda_{\phi}[H_{1}(Y)]\to{{\mathbb{Z}}}[t^{-1},t]] is the map induced by the projection ϕ:H1​(Y)→ℤ\phi:H_{1}(Y)\to{{\mathbb{Z}}}, we define

τ¯​(Y)=Φ⁡(τ⁡(Y))andΔ¯​(Y)=(1−t)​τ¯​(Y).\overline{\tau}(Y)=\Phi(\tau(Y))\quad\text{and}\quad\overline{\Delta}(Y)=(1-t)\overline{\tau}(Y).

Note that in general, Δ¯​(Y)≠Δ​(Y)\overline{\Delta}(Y)\neq\Delta(Y); an interesting example to consider is the connected sum Y=Z​#​(S1×D2)Y=Z\mkern 1.5mu\#\mkern 1.5mu(S^{1}\mkern-2.0mu\times\mkern-2.0muD^{2}), where b1​(Z)=0b_{1}(Z)=0. This manifold has Δ⁡(Y)=0\Delta(Y)=0, but Δ¯​(Y)=|H1​(Z)|\overline{\Delta}(Y)=|H_{1}(Z)|.

If KK is a knot in S3S^{3}, it is well known that deg⁡Δ⁡(t)≤2​g​(K)\deg\Delta(t)\leq 2g(K), and Δ⁡(K)|t=1=1\Delta(K)|_{t=1}=1. The following result is a simultaneous generalization of these two facts.

Proposition 2.2 ([45] Lemma II.4.5.1 and Theorem II.4.2.1).

If ‖Y‖\|Y\| is the Thurston norm of a generator of H2​(Y,∂Y)H_{2}(Y,\partial Y) and τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) is normalized as above, then ah=1a_{h}=1 for all h∈H1​(Y)h\in H_{1}(Y) with ϕ⁡(h)>‖Y‖\phi(h)>\|Y\|.

More generally, it is known that H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) determines both the Thurston norm of YY and whether it is fibred [35, 34, 26]. Since the knot Floer homology of a Floer simple knot is determined by its Euler characteristic, we have

Corollary 2.3.

If YY is boundary incompressible and Floer simple, ‖Y‖=deg⁡Δ¯​(Y)−1\|Y\|=\deg\overline{\Delta}(Y)-1. If YY is also irreducible, then YY fibres over S1S^{1} if and only if Δ¯​(Y)\overline{\Delta}(Y) is monic.

2.2. Differentials

The knot Floer homology of KK can be used to compute the Floer homology of surgeries on KK. Before we explain how to do this, we must understand the relation between H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) and H​F^​(Y¯){{\widehat{HF}}}(\overline{Y}).

We begin by discussing Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} structures. There are maps iv,ih:Spinc​(Y,∂Y)→Spinc​(Y¯)i_{v},i_{h}:{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y)\to{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(\overline{Y}) which respect the action of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y), in the sense that iv​(𝔰+a)=iv​(𝔰)+i∗​(a)i_{v}(\mathfrak{s}+a)=i_{v}(\mathfrak{s})+i_{*}(a) and ih​(𝔰+a)=ih​(𝔰)+i∗​(a)i_{h}(\mathfrak{s}+a)=i_{h}(\mathfrak{s})+i_{*}(a) where i∗:H1​(Y)→H1​(Y¯)i_{*}:H_{1}(Y)\to H_{1}(\overline{Y}) is the map induced by inclusion. Moreover, iv​(𝔰)−ih​(𝔰)=i∗​(λ)i_{v}(\mathfrak{s})-i_{h}(\mathfrak{s})=i_{*}(\lambda), where λ\lambda is a longitude of KK. We define an equivalence relation on Spinc​(Y,∂Y){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) by declaring 𝔰1∼𝔰2\mathfrak{s}_{1}\sim\mathfrak{s}_{2} if iv​(𝔰1)=iv​(𝔰2)i_{v}(\mathfrak{s}_{1})=i_{v}(\mathfrak{s}_{2}). It is easy to see that this is the same as requiring that ih​(𝔰1)=ih​(𝔰2)i_{h}(\mathfrak{s}_{1})=i_{h}(\mathfrak{s}_{2}), and that the equivalence classes are orbits of Spinc​(Y,∂Y){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) under the action of μ\mu.

Let 𝔰~\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}} be an equivalence class in Spinc​(Y,∂Y){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y). After we choose some auxiliary data (a doubly pointed Heegaard diagram for KK), Heegaard Floer homology constructs for us a graded group

C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)=⨁𝔰∈𝔰~C​F​K^​(K,𝔰)\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}})=\bigoplus_{\mathfrak{s}\in\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}}\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s})

together with maps d0,dv,dh:C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)→C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)d_{0},d_{v},d_{h}:\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}})\to\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}), which are filtered with respect to the Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} grading in the following sense: if x∈C​F​K^​(Y,𝔰)x\in\widehat{CFK}(Y,\mathfrak{s}), then d0​x∈C​F​K^​(Y,𝔰)d_{0}x\in\widehat{CFK}(Y,\mathfrak{s}), dvx∈⊕k<0C​F​K^(Y,𝔰+kμ)d_{v}x\in\oplus_{k<0}\widehat{CFK}(Y,\mathfrak{s}+k\mu) and dhx∈⊕k>0C​F​K^(Y,𝔰+kμ).d_{h}x\in\oplus_{k>0}\widehat{CFK}(Y,\mathfrak{s}+k\mu). These differentials satisfy the relations d02=(d0+dv)2=(d0+dh)2=0d_{0}^{2}=(d_{0}+d_{v})^{2}=(d_{0}+d_{h})^{2}=0. Furthermore, we have

H​(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰),d0)\displaystyle H(\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}),d_{0}) =H​F​K^​(K,𝔰),\displaystyle=\widehat{HFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}),
H⁡(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dv)\displaystyle H(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{v}) =H​F​K^​(Y¯,iv​(𝔰)),\displaystyle=\widehat{HFK}(\overline{Y},i_{v}(\mathfrak{s})),
H⁡(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dh)\displaystyle H(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{h}) =H​F​K^​(Y¯,ih​(𝔰)).\displaystyle=\widehat{HFK}(\overline{Y},i_{h}(\mathfrak{s})).

The Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} grading provides a natural filtration on the latter two complexes, in the sense that ⊕k<nC​F​K^(K,𝔰+kμ)\oplus_{k<n}\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}+k\mu) is a subcomplex of (C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dv)(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{v}) and ⊕k>nC​F​K^(K,𝔰+kμ)\oplus_{k>n}\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}+k\mu) is a subcomplex of (C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dh)(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{h}). These filtrations give rise to spectral sequences whose E1E_{1} term is H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}). We denote by d~v,d~h\tilde{d}_{v},\tilde{d}_{h} the induced differentials on the E1E_{1} term, so that e.g. C​F​K^​(K,d0+dv)\widehat{CFK}(K,d_{0}+d_{v}) is homotopy equivalent to H​F​K^​(K,d~v)\widehat{HFK}(K,\tilde{d}_{v}). (Note that these are not the same as the d1d_{1} differentials in the spectral sequence.)

Definition 2.4.

For each 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y), the bent complex is AK,𝔰=(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d𝔰)A_{K,\mathfrak{s}}=(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{\mathfrak{s}}), where for x∈C​F​K^​(K,𝔰+k​μ)x\in\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}+k\mu),

d𝔰​(x)={d0​(x)+dv​(x)k<0d0​(x)+dv​(x)+dh​(x)k=0d0​(x)+dh​(x)k>0.d_{\mathfrak{s}}(x)=\begin{cases}d_{0}(x)+d_{v}(x)\quad&k<0\\ d_{0}(x)+d_{v}(x)+d_{h}(x)\quad&k=0\\ d_{0}(x)+d_{h}(x)\quad&k>0\end{cases}.

The bent complexes measure the Heegaard Floer homology of large integer surgery on KK: H⁡(AK,𝔰)≃H​F^​(Y⁡(N​μ+λ),in​(𝔰))H(A_{K,\mathfrak{s}})\simeq{{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(N\mu+\lambda),i_{n}(\mathfrak{s})) for sufficiently large NN and an appropriately chosen Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} structure iN​(𝔰)i_{N}(\mathfrak{s}) on the filling.

The existence of the Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} filtration means there are chain maps

πv\displaystyle\pi_{v} :AK,𝔰→(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dv)\displaystyle:A_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\to(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{v})
πh\displaystyle\pi_{h} :AK,𝔰→(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dh)\displaystyle:A_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\to(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{h})

given by

πv​(x)={0k>0xk≤0πh​(x)={xk≥00k<0\pi_{v}(x)=\begin{cases}0\quad&k>0\\ x\quad&k\leq 0\end{cases}\quad\quad\pi_{h}(x)=\begin{cases}x\quad&k\geq 0\\ 0\quad&k<0\end{cases}

for x∈C​F​K^​(𝔰+k​μ)x\in\widehat{CFK}(\mathfrak{s}+k\mu).

2.3. The Ozsváth-Szabó mapping cone

Let λ\lambda be a longitude for KK, so that μ⋅λ=1\mu\cdot\lambda=1. The mapping cone of Ozsváth and Szabó [40] relates the Heegaard Floer homology of the filling Y⁡(λ)Y(\lambda) to the knot Floer homology of KK. We recall its construction here.

Since ih​(𝔰−λ)=iv​(𝔰)i_{h}(\mathfrak{s}-\lambda)=i_{v}(\mathfrak{s}), we have

H⁡(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰−λ),d0+dh)≃H​F^​(Y,iv​(𝔰))≃H⁡(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰),d0+dv).H(\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}-\lambda),d_{0}+d_{h})\simeq{{\widehat{HF}}}(Y,i_{v}(\mathfrak{s}))\simeq H(\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}),d_{0}+d_{v}).

This isomorphism is realized by a chain homotopy equivalence

j:(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰−λ),d0+dh)→(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰),d0+dv).j:(\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}-\lambda),d_{0}+d_{h})\to(\widehat{CFK}(K,\mathfrak{s}),d_{0}+d_{v}).

(The map on homology induced by jj is the canonical isomorphism of [27], although we will not use this fact here.)

For 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y,∂Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y), let BK,𝔰=(C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~),d0+dv)B_{K,\mathfrak{s}}=(\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}),d_{0}+d_{v}). We form two chain complexes

𝔸⁡(K)=⨁𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)AK,𝔰and𝔹⁡(K)=⨁𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)BK,𝔰.\mathbb{A}(K)=\bigoplus_{\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y)}A_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{B}(K)=\bigoplus_{\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y)}B_{K,\mathfrak{s}}.

There is a chain map fλ:𝔸⁡(K)→𝔹⁡(K)f_{\lambda}:\mathbb{A}(K)\to\mathbb{B}(K) given by f=πv+j∘πhf=\pi_{v}+j\circ\pi_{h}. (So if x∈AK,𝔰x\in A_{K,\mathfrak{s}}, fλ​(x)f_{\lambda}(x) is a sum of terms in BK,𝔰B_{K,\mathfrak{s}} and BK,𝔰+λB_{K,\mathfrak{s}+\lambda}.) Let 𝕏λ​(K)\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K) be the mapping cone of fλf_{\lambda}. In [40] , Ozsváth and Szabó prove

Theorem 2.5.

[40] H​F^​(Y⁡(λ))≃H∗​(𝕏λ​(K)){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda))\simeq H_{*}(\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K)).

We make some remarks on the construction. First, it is easy to see that the complex 𝕏λ​(K)\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K) decomposes as a direct sum of complexes whose underlying groups are of the form

𝕏λ​(K,𝔰)=⨁n∈ℤAK,𝔰+n​λ⊕⨁n∈ℤBK,𝔰+n​λ.\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K,\mathfrak{s})=\bigoplus_{n\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}}A_{K,\mathfrak{s}+n\lambda}\oplus\bigoplus_{n\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}}B_{K,\mathfrak{s}+n\lambda}.

The summands are on one to one correspondence with elements of the quotient H1​(Y)/⟨λ⟩≃H1​(Y⁡(λ))H_{1}(Y)/\langle\lambda\rangle\simeq H_{1}(Y(\lambda)). The resulting decomposition on homology corresponds to the decomposition of H​F^​(Y​(λ)){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda)) by Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} structures.

Second, if 𝔽p{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} is the field of order pp, where pp is a prime, then we can form the complex 𝕏λ​(K,𝔽p)=𝕏λ​(K)⊗𝔽p\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K;{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}})=\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K)\otimes{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}. It follows from the universal coefficient theorem that H​F^​(Y⁡(λ),𝔽p)≃H∗​(𝕏λ​(K,𝔽p)){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda);{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}})\simeq H_{*}(\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K;{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}})).

Finally, it is often convenient to work with the homology of the complexes AK,𝔰A_{K,\mathfrak{s}} and BK,𝔰B_{K,\mathfrak{s}}, rather than the complexes themselves. We can do this if we use field coefficients. Specifically, fix a field 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, and let 𝐀K,𝔰=H⁡(AK,𝔰⊗𝔽p)\mathbf{A}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}=H(A_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{p}), 𝐀⁡(K)=⊕𝐀K,𝔰\mathbf{A}(K)=\oplus\mathbf{A}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}, 𝐁K,𝔰=H⁡(BK,𝔰⊗𝔽p)\mathbf{B}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}=H(B_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\otimes\mathbb{F}_{p}), 𝐁⁡(K)=⊕𝐁K,𝔰\mathbf{B}(K)=\oplus\mathbf{B}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}. Similarly, let v:𝐀K,𝔰→𝐁K,𝔰v:\mathbf{A}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\to\mathbf{B}_{K,\mathfrak{s}} be the map induced by πv\pi_{v}, and h:𝐀K,𝔰→𝐁K,𝔰+λh:\mathbf{A}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\to\mathbf{B}_{K,\mathfrak{s}+\lambda} be the map induced by j∘πhj\circ\pi_{h}. Finally, let Cλ​(K,𝔽p)C_{\lambda}(K;\mathbb{F}_{p}) be the chain complex whose underlying group is 𝐀⁡(K)⊕𝐁⁡(K)\mathbf{A}(K)\oplus\mathbf{B}(K), with differential given by d​x=v⁡(x)+h⁡(x)dx=v(x)+h(x) for x∈𝐀⁡(K)x\in\mathbf{A}(K), d​y=0dy=0 for y∈𝐁⁡(K)y\in\mathbf{B}(K).

Corollary 2.6.

H​F^​(Y⁡(λ),𝔽p)≃H⁡(Cλ​(K,𝔽p)){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda);\mathbb{F}_{p})\simeq H(C_{\lambda}(K;\mathbb{F}_{p})).

Proof.

The short exact sequence

0→𝔹⁡(K)⊗𝔽p→𝕏λ​(K,𝔽p)→𝔸⁡(K)⊗𝔽p→00\to\mathbb{B}(K)\otimes\mathbb{F}_{p}\to\mathbb{X}_{\lambda}(K;\mathbb{F}_{p})\to\mathbb{A}(K)\otimes\mathbb{F}_{p}\to 0

gives a long exact sequence

→𝐁⁡(K)→H​F^​(Y⁡(λ),𝔽p)→𝐀⁡(K)→𝐁⁡(K)→\to\mathbf{B}(K)\to{{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda);\mathbb{F}_{p})\to\mathbf{A}(K)\to\mathbf{B}(K)\to

whose boundary map is given by v+hv+h. An exact sequence over a field splits, so we get the statement of the corollary. ∎

2.4. Splicing and surgery

Suppose Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} are rational homology solid tori, and that φ:∂Y1→∂Y2\varphi:\partial Y_{1}\to\partial Y_{2} is an orientation reversing diffeomorphism. The manifold Yφ=Y1∪φY2Y_{\varphi}=Y_{1}\cup_{\varphi}Y_{2} is obtained by splicing Y1Y_{1} and Y2Y_{2} together along φ\varphi. Choose a slope μ1∈S​l​(∂Y1)\mu_{1}\in Sl(\partial Y_{1}), and let μ2=φ∗​(μ)\mu_{2}=\varphi_{*}(\mu) be its image in S​l​(∂Y2)Sl(\partial Y_{2}). Let Y¯i=Yi​(μi)\overline{Y}_{i}=Y_{i}(\mu_{i}) be the corresponding Dehn fillings, and let Ki=KμiK_{i}=K_{\mu_{i}} be their cores.

Lemma 2.7.

YφY_{\varphi} can be obtained by integral surgery on K1​#​K2⊂Y¯1​#​Y¯2K_{1}\#K_{2}\subset\overline{Y}_{1}\#\overline{Y}_{2}.

This is well-known, but an understanding of the proof will be useful in what follows, so we sketch it here.

Proof.

Let Y′Y^{\prime} be the complement of K1​#​K2K_{1}\#K_{2}. Y′Y^{\prime} is obtained by identifying an annulus ν⁡(μ1)⊂∂Y1\nu(\mu_{1})\subset\partial Y_{1} with its image ν⁡(μ2)=φ⁡(ν⁡(μ1))⊂∂Y2\nu(\mu_{2})=\varphi(\nu(\mu_{1}))\subset\partial Y_{2}. (Throughout the proof, we use the same symbol to denote both a slope on the torus and a simple closed curve representing it.) Equivalently, Y′Y^{\prime} can be obtained by starting with the disjoint union of Y1,Y2Y_{1},Y_{2} and S1×I×IS^{1}\times I\times I and identifying S1×I×0S^{1}\times I\times 0 with ν⁡(μ1)\nu(\mu_{1}) and S1×I×1S^{1}\times I\times 1 with ν⁡(μ2)\nu(\mu_{2}). In this model, ∂Y′\partial Y^{\prime} is a union of four annuli: ∂Y1−ν⁡(μ1)\partial Y_{1}-\nu(\mu_{1}), S1×0×IS^{1}\times 0\times I, ∂Y2−ν⁡(μ2)\partial Y_{2}-\nu(\mu_{2}), and S1×1×IS^{1}\times 1\times I. The meridian μ\mu of K1​#​K2K_{1}\#K_{2} is homotopic to both μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} (and to the core of each of the four annuli.)

Let λ1\lambda_{1} be a longitude for μ1\mu_{1}, so that λ2=−φ⁡(λ1)\lambda_{2}=-\varphi(\lambda_{1}) is a longitude for μ2\mu_{2}. We may assume that λ1∩ν⁡(μ1)=p×I⊂S1×I≃ν⁡(μ1)\lambda_{1}\cap\nu(\mu_{1})=p\times I\subset S^{1}\times I\simeq\nu(\mu_{1}), and similarly for λ2\lambda_{2}. Let λ1′\lambda_{1}^{\prime} be the arc obtained by intersecting λ1\lambda_{1} with ∂Y1−ν⁡(μ1)\partial Y_{1}-\nu(\mu_{1}), and similarly for λ2′\lambda_{2}^{\prime}. The union of the arcs λ1′,p×0×I,λ2′,\lambda_{1}^{\prime},p\times 0\times I,\lambda_{2}^{\prime}, and p×1×Ip\times 1\times I is a longitude λ\lambda for K1​#​K2K_{1}\#K_{2}. Attaching a 2-handle along λ\lambda is the same as attaching I×I×II\times I\times I to Y′Y^{\prime}, where the top and bottom edges I×1/2×1I\times 1/2\times 1 and I×1/2×0I\times 1/2\times 0 are identified with λ1′\lambda_{1}^{\prime} and λ2′\lambda_{2}^{\prime}, and the sides 1×1/2×I1\times 1/2\times I and 0×1/2×I0\times 1/2\times I are identified with the other arcs in λ\lambda. The resulting manifold can be obtained by starting with Y1,Y2Y_{1},Y_{2} and Σ×I\Sigma\times I, where Σ\Sigma is a regular neighborhood of the 11-skeleton in T2T^{2} and identifying Σ×0\Sigma\times 0 with a tubular neighborhood of μ1∪λ1⊂∂Y1\mu_{1}\cup\lambda_{1}\subset\partial Y_{1} and Σ×1\Sigma\times 1 with its image under φ\varphi. Finally, filling in the spherical boundary component with B3B^{3} gives Y1∪(T2×I)∪Y2=YφY_{1}\cup(T^{2}\times I)\cup Y_{2}=Y_{\varphi}. ∎

From the proof, we see that H1​(Y′)≃H1​(Y1)⊕H1​(Y2)/RH_{1}(Y^{\prime})\simeq H_{1}(Y_{1})\oplus H_{1}(Y_{2})/R, where RR is the subgroup generated by (μ1,μ2)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}), and that under this isomorphism, λ=(λ1,φ∗​(λ1))=(λ1,−λ2)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\varphi_{*}(\lambda_{1}))=(\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2}).

We make two remarks on the utility of this construction. First, it is quite flexible, in the sense that the choice of any meridian μ1∈S​l​(∂Y1)\mu_{1}\in Sl(\partial Y_{1}) gives a different way of realizing the spliced manifold as a surgery. This flexibility will be useful to us in what follows.

Second, rational surgery on a knot K⊂Y¯K\subset\overline{Y} amounts to splicing YY with S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}. Suppose ⟨μ,λ⟩\langle\mu,\lambda\rangle is our usual basis for H1​(∂Y)H_{1}(\partial Y), and that ⟨m,l⟩\langle m,l\rangle is the standard basis for H1​(∂S1×D2)H_{1}(\partial S^{1}\times D^{2}) (so l=[∂D2]l=[\partial D^{2}]). If we glue ∂Y\partial Y to ∂(S1×D2)\partial(S^{1}\times D^{2}) in such a way that [∂D2][\partial D^{2}] is identified with α=p​μ+q​λ∈H1​(∂Y)\alpha=p\mu+q\lambda\in H_{1}(\partial Y), then it is easy to see that μ\mu is identified with −q​m+p∗​l-qm+p^{*}l, where p​p∗≡1​mod​qpp^{*}\equiv 1\,{{\mathrm{mod\;}}}q. Applying the lemma, we see that Y⁡(α)Y(\alpha) is obtained by integer surgery on a knot K′=K#K−q/p⊂Y¯#L(q,−p∗)=Y¯#L(q,−p)K^{\prime}=K\#K_{-q/p}\subset\overline{Y}\#L(q,-p^{*})=\overline{Y}\#L(q,-p).

The knot K−q/pK_{-q/p} is the unique knot in L⁡(q,−p)L(q,-p) whose complement is S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}. (In the notation of [44], it is the simple knot K⁡(q,−p,1)K(q,-p,1)). It is Floer simple, with Euler characteristic

χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K⁡(q,−p,1))∼tq−1t−1CLOSE.\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K(q,-p,1))\sim\frac{t^{q}-1}{t-1}.

To use Lemma 2.7 to compute the Floer homology of a splice, we need to know how the knot Floer homology behaves under connected sum.

Lemma 2.8.

[41] H​F​K^​(K1​#​K2)≃H​F​K^​(K1)⊗H​F​K^​(K2)\widehat{HFK}(K_{1}\#K_{2})\simeq\widehat{HFK}(K_{1})\otimes\widehat{HFK}(K_{2}).

The isomorphism is well-behaved with respect to Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} structures, in the sense that

χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K1​#​K2))∼χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K1))​χ​(H​F​K^​(K2)).\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K_{1}\#K_{2}))\sim\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K_{1}))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K_{2})).

It is also respects the differentials, in the sense that C​F​K^​(K1​#​K2,d0+dv)\widehat{CFK}(K_{1}\#K_{2},d_{0}+d_{v}) is homotopy equivalent to C​F​K^​(K1,d0+dv)⊗C​F​K^​(K2,d0+dv)\widehat{CFK}(K_{1},d_{0}+d_{v})\otimes\widehat{CFK}(K_{2},d_{0}+d_{v}), and similarly for dhd_{h}.

In [41], Ozsváth and Szabó combined the observations above with their mapping cone for integer surgeries to express the Floer homology of any rational surgery as a mapping cone.

3. Floer Simple Manifolds

In this section we use Ozsváth and Szabó’s mapping cone formula to prove Proposition 1.3 and to derive some basic facts about Floer simple manifolds. For the most part, these are straightforward extensions of results in [39],[44], and [4]. We conclude by explaining how to compute the bordered Floer homology of a Floer simple manifold YY in terms of τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) and a Floer simple filling slope α\alpha. Our notation and assumptions are the same as in section 2.

3.1. Proof of Proposition 1.3

Suppose that K⊂Y¯K\subset\overline{Y} is a knot in an LL–space, and that some nontrivial surgery on YY is also an L-space.

Definition 3.1.

We say that H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}) is a positive chain if it is generated by elements x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n-1} and the induced differentials d~h\tilde{d}_{h}, d~v\tilde{d}_{v} satisfy d~v​(yi)=±xi+1\tilde{d}_{v}(y_{i})=\pm x_{i+1}, d~h​(yi)=±xi+1\tilde{d}_{h}(y_{i})=\pm x_{i+1}, and d~v​(xi)=d~h​(xi)=0\tilde{d}_{v}(x_{i})=\tilde{d}_{h}(x_{i})=0 for all ii. More generally, we say that H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) consists of positive chains if C​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)\widehat{CFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}) is a positive chain for each 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y), and that H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) consists of coherent chains if either H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) or H​F​K^​(−K)\widehat{HFK}(-K) consists of positive chains, where −K⊂−Y¯-K\subset-\overline{Y} is the mirror knot.

Note that all the xix_{i}’s in the definition must have the same relative ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading, which is opposite that of the yiy_{i}’s. Since there are more xix_{i}’s than yiy_{i}’s, the xix_{i} contribute to χ​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K)) with positive sign, while the yiy_{i}’s contribute with negative sign.

Ozsváth and Szabó proved in [39] that if K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} has an L-space surgery with positive slope, then H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is a positive chain. The following generalization is an easy consequence of a result of Boileau, Boyer, Cebanu, and Walsh:

Lemma 3.2.

Suppose that K⊂Y¯K\subset\overline{Y} is a knot in an LL–space, and that some surgery on KK is also an LL–space. Then H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) consists of coherent chains.

Proof.

A surgery on KK is positive if the corresponding surgery cobordism is positive definite. Suppose that some positive integral surgery on KK is an L-space. By Lemma 6.7 of [4], the bent group AK,𝔰≃ℤA_{K,\mathfrak{s}}\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}} for all 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y,∂Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y). The proof of Theorem 1.2 of [39] carries over unchanged to show that H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~)\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}) is a positive chain.

Next, suppose that Y′Y^{\prime} is obtained by negative integral surgery on K⊂Y¯K\subset\overline{Y}, and that Y′Y^{\prime} is an L-space. By reversing the orientation of the surgery cobordism, we see that −Y′-Y^{\prime} is obtained by positive surgery on −K⊂−Y¯-K\subset-\overline{Y}. −Y′-Y^{\prime} is also an L-space, so H​F​K^​(−K)\widehat{HFK}(-K) consists of positive chains, and H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) consists of negative ones.

Finally, suppose that an L-space Y′Y^{\prime} is obtained by fractional surgery on KK. Then Y′Y^{\prime} is obtained by integral surgery on a knot of the form K#K−q/p⊂Y¯#L(q,−p)K\#K_{-q/p}\subset\overline{Y}\#L(q,-p), so H​F​K^(K#K−q/p)≃H​F​K^(K)⊗H​F​K^(K−q/p)\widehat{HFK}(K\#K_{-q/p})\simeq\widehat{HFK}(K)\otimes\widehat{HFK}(K_{-q/p}) is composed of coherent chains. Since K−q/pK_{-q/p} is Floer simple, it is easy to see that this occurs if and only if H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of coherent chains. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

If H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) consists of coherent chains, then τ⁡(Y)=∑h∈S⁡[τ⁡(Y)][h].\displaystyle\tau(Y)=\sum_{h\in S[\tau(Y)]}[h].

Proof.

We have

τ⁡(Y)∼χ​(H​F​K^​(K))(1−[μ])=(∑𝔰¯∈Mχ⁡(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~))​𝔰¯)​(∑i=0∞[μ]i)\tau(Y)\sim\frac{\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K))}{(1-[\mu])}=\left(\sum_{\overline{\mathfrak{s}}\in M}\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}))\overline{\mathfrak{s}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}[\mu]^{i}\right)

where M⊂Spinc​(Y,∂Y)M\subset{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) is a set of coset representatives for the action of ⟨μ⟩\langle\mu\rangle and

χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~))=∑j∈ℤχ⁡(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰¯+j​μ))​[μ]j.\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}))=\sum_{j\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}}\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\overline{\mathfrak{s}}+j\mu))[\mu]^{j}.

The hypothesis that H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) consists of coherent chains implies that the nonzero coefficients of χ​(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}})) alternate between +1+1 and −1-1, and that the outermost coefficients are +1+1. It follows that the coefficients of the product χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K,𝔰~))​(∑i=0∞[μ]i)\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K,\widetilde{\mathfrak{s}}))\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}[\mu]^{i}\right) are all either 00 or +1+1, and hence that all the coefficients of τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) are either 00 or 11 as well. ∎

Corollary 3.4.

Suppose H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of coherent chains, and that ϕ⁡(μ)>‖Y‖\phi(\mu)>\|Y\|. Then KK is Floer simple.

Proof.

By hypothesis, H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of coherent chains, so to prove that KK is Floer simple, it suffices to show that every monomial in χ​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K)) appears with a positive coefficient. As usual, we normalize τ⁡(Y)=∑hah​[h]\tau(Y)=\sum_{h}a_{h}[h] so that ah=0a_{h}=0 whenever ϕ⁡(h)<0\phi(h)<0, and a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0. We have χ⁡(H​F​K^​(K))∼(1−[μ])​τ​(Y),\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K))\sim(1-[\mu])\tau(Y), so the coefficient of [h][h] in χ​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K)) is ah−ah−μa_{h}-a_{h-\mu}. Both terms in this difference are either 00 or 11. If ϕ⁡(μ)>ϕ⁡(h)\phi(\mu)>\phi(h), then ah−μ=0a_{h-\mu}=0, while if ϕ⁡(h)≥ϕ⁡(μ)>‖Y‖\phi(h)\geq\phi(\mu)>\|Y\|, then ah=1a_{h}=1 by Proposition 2.2. In either case, we see that the coefficient of [h][h] in χ​(H​F​K^​(K))\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K)) is either 00 or 11. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

If H​F​K^​(Y)\widehat{HFK}(Y) is composed of positive chains, there is an interval in S​l​(Y)Sl(Y) whose left endpoint is μ\mu and which is contained in ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y).

Proof.

Since H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of positive chains, the homology of each of its bent complexes is ℤ{{\mathbb{Z}}}. Since the homology of the bent complexes computes H​F^​(Y​(N​μ+λ)){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(N\mu+\lambda)) for some N≫0N\gg 0, we see that N​μ+λ∈ℒ⁡(Y)N\mu+\lambda\in\mathcal{L}(Y). Since μ⋅(N​μ+λ)=1\mu\cdot(N\mu+\lambda)=1, Proposition 17 of [7] shows that the entire interval [μ,N​μ+λ][\mu,N\mu+\lambda] is contained in ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). ∎

By considering mirrors, we see that if H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of negative chains, then μ\mu is the right endpoint of a closed interval in ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). It follows that if KK is Floer simple, then it is an interior point of an interval in ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). Conversely, if H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of negative chains but is not Floer simple, then some bent group of KK has rank >1>1. This implies that Y⁡(N​μ+λ)Y(N\mu+\lambda) is not an L-space for N≫0N\gg 0. Thus if H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of coherent chains but is not Floer simple, μ\mu is in not in the interior of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y).

Proof.

(Of Proposition 1.3) If YY is Floer simple, then it has some filling Y⁡(α)Y(\alpha) for which KαK_{\alpha} is Floer simple. As we observed above, α\alpha is contained in the interior of an interval in ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y), so clearly |ℒ⁡(Y)|>1|\mathcal{L}(Y)|>1. Conversely, if ℒ⁡(Y)>1\mathcal{L}(Y)>1, then H​F​K^​(K)\widehat{HFK}(K) is composed of coherent chains, so ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y) contains an interval. Now any interval in S​l​(Y)Sl(Y) contains elements α\alpha with ϕ⁡(α)\phi(\alpha) arbitrarily large. (To see this, identify S​l​(Y)Sl(Y) with ℚ¯\overline{{{\mathbb{Q}}}} using the canonical meridian and longitude. If α↦a/b\alpha\mapsto a/b under this identification, then ϕ⁡(α)=k​a\phi(\alpha)=ka for some fixed k>0k>0.) By Corollary 3.4, Kα⊂Y⁡(α)K_{\alpha}\subset Y(\alpha) is Floer simple, so YY is Floer simple. ∎

3.2. Surgery on Floer simple knots

We now suppose that K⊂Y¯K\subset\overline{Y} is Floer simple. We give a graphical criterion for determining whether a given integer surgery on KK is an L-space. To do so, we consider the set Sblack=S⁡[H​F​K^​(K)]⊂Spinc​(Y,∂Y){{S_{\textsc{black}}}}=S[\widehat{HFK}(K)]\subset{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y). Since KK is Floer simple, Sblack{{S_{\textsc{black}}}} is a set of coset representatives for the action of the subgroup ⟨μ⟩⊂H1​(Y)\langle\mu\rangle\subset H_{1}(Y). In other words, every 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y,∂Y)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) can be written in a unique way as 𝔰¯+n​μ\overline{\mathfrak{s}}+n\mu, where 𝔰¯∈Sblack\overline{\mathfrak{s}}\in{{S_{\textsc{black}}}} and n∈ℤn\in{{\mathbb{Z}}}. We color 𝔰\mathfrak{s} black if n=0n=0, red if n>0n>0, and blue if n<0n<0.

Now suppose we do surgery along KK with slope λ\lambda, where μ⋅λ=1\mu\cdot\lambda=1. We divide Spinc​(Y,∂Y){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\partial Y) into cosets for the action of ⟨λ⟩\langle\lambda\rangle. Each coset LL is an affine copy of ℤ{{\mathbb{Z}}}, so it has a natural ordering. Each element of LL is colored either black, red, or blue; elements which are sufficiently negative are all colored blue, and elements which are sufficiently positive are all colored red. We say LL is properly colored if no red element of LL appears before a blue element.

Proposition 3.6.

Y⁡(λ)Y(\lambda) is an L-space if and only if every coset for the action of ⟨λ⟩\langle\lambda\rangle is properly colored.

Proof.

The argument is the same as the proof of Lemma 4.8 in [44]; we sketch it briefly here. We fix a prime pp and use the mapping cone to compute H​F^​(Y​(λ),𝔽p){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda);{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}). The mapping cone Cλ​(K)C_{\lambda}(K) decomposes as a direct sum of chain complexes CLC_{L}, one for each coset LL. Since KK is Floer simple, the bent groups 𝐀K,𝔰¯+n​λ\mathbf{A}_{K,\overline{\mathfrak{s}}+n\lambda} appearing in one summand are all isomorphic to 𝔽p{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}, as are the groups 𝐁K,𝔰¯+n​λ\mathbf{B}_{K,\overline{\mathfrak{s}}+n\lambda}. Let h𝔰,v𝔰h_{\mathfrak{s}},v_{\mathfrak{s}} be the restriction of the maps h,vh,v to 𝐀K,𝔰\mathbf{A}_{K,\mathfrak{s}}. If 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is colored red, the map v𝔰v_{\mathfrak{s}} is an isomorphism and h𝔰=0h_{\mathfrak{s}}=0; if 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is colored blue, the map h𝔰h_{\mathfrak{s}} is an isomorphism and v𝔰=0v_{\mathfrak{s}}=0; and if 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is colored black, both h𝔰h_{\mathfrak{s}} and v𝔰v_{\mathfrak{s}} are isomorphisms.

The complex CLC_{L} takes the form shown in Figure 1, where each colored dot in the top row represents 𝐀K,𝔰¯+n​λ≃𝔽p\mathbf{A}_{K,\overline{\mathfrak{s}}+n\lambda}\simeq{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}, each dot in the bottom row represents 𝐁K,𝔰¯+n​λ≃𝔽p\mathbf{B}_{K,\overline{\mathfrak{s}}+n\lambda}\simeq{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}, and the arrows represent nonzero differentials. The chain of differentials breaks each time we encounter a red or blue dot, thus decomposing CLC_{L} into smaller summands. Summands corresponding to intervals in LL whose endpoints are both red or both blue are acyclic; summands whose left endpoint is blue and whose right endpoint is red have homology in even ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 homological degree, and summands whose left endpoint is red and whose right endpoint is blue have homology in odd ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 homological degree.

It follows that H​F^​(Y⁡(λ),𝔰¯)≃𝔽p{{\widehat{HF}}}(Y(\lambda),\overline{\mathfrak{s}})\simeq{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} if and only if LL is properly colored, and hence that Y⁡(λ)Y(\lambda) is an 𝔽p{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} L-space if and only if every coset is properly colored. Finally, the statement of the proposition follows from the fact that Y⁡(λ)Y(\lambda) is an L-space if and only it is an 𝔽p{{\mathbb{F}}_{p}} L-space for every prime pp. ∎

3.3. Bordered Floer homology of Floer simple manifolds

In this section, we show that the bordered Floer homology [29] of a Floer simple manifold YY is determined by the Turaev torsion of YY together with a slope in the interior of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). We very briefly review some facts about bordered Floer homology; for more details see [29, 30].

A bordered three-manifold is an oriented three-manifold YY equipped with a parametrization (that is, a minimal handle decomposition) of its boundary. We will restrict our attention to the case where ∂Y=T2\partial Y=T^{2}, in which case a parametrization is specified by a choice of two simple closed curves μ,λ∈H1​(∂Y)\mu,\lambda\in H_{1}(\partial Y) which satisfy μ⋅λ=1\mu\cdot\lambda=1.

The type DD bordered Floer homology C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) is a differential graded module over a certain 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}–algebra 𝒜⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z}) associated to the torus. 𝒜⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z}) is generated by elements ρ1,ρ2,ρ3,ρ12,ρ23\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{3},\rho_{12},\rho_{23} and ρ123\rho_{123} corresponding to certain arcs on the boundary of the 00-handle in the handle decomposition of ∂Y\partial Y, together with a pair of idempotents ι0,ι1\iota_{0},\iota_{1}. Following Chapter 11 of [29], we can think of the module structure as being specified by a pair of vector spaces V0V^{0}, V1V^{1} over the field of two elements 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, together with linear maps

D1,D3,D123\displaystyle D_{1},D_{3},D_{123} :V0→V1\displaystyle:V^{0}\to V^{1}\quad\quad D2:V1→V0\displaystyle D_{2}:V^{1}\to V^{0}
D12\displaystyle D_{12} :V0→V0\displaystyle:V^{0}\to V^{0}\quad\quad D23:V1→V1\displaystyle D_{23}:V^{1}\to V^{1}

where C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)=𝒜⁡(𝒵)⊗𝔽2(V0⊕V1)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda)=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z})\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(V^{0}\oplus V^{1}) and for x∈V0⊕V1x\in V^{0}\oplus V^{1}, the differential is given by ∂x=∑ρI​DI​(x).\partial x=\sum\rho_{I}D_{I}(x).

In writing the above, we have assumed that C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) has been reduced with respect to all provincial differentials, so that

V0≃S​F​H​(Y,γμ)≃H​F​K^​(Kμ)V1≃H​F​K^​(Y,γλ)≃H​F​K​(Kλ)V^{0}\simeq SFH(Y,\gamma_{\mu})\simeq\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu})\quad V^{1}\simeq\widehat{HFK}(Y,\gamma_{\lambda})\simeq HFK(K_{\lambda})

where the suture γμ\gamma_{\mu} is two parallel copies of μ\mu, and similarly for γλ\gamma_{\lambda}.

Petkova [42] showed that the algebra 𝒜⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z}) can be given an absolute ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading, and that C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) can be given a ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading compatible with it. Petkova’s grading depends on some auxiliary choices, but we can make some statements which are independent of these choices.

Lemma 3.7.

The maps D12D_{12} and D23D_{23} preserve the homological ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading. If D1D_{1} has parity ii with respect to the ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading, then D2D_{2}, D3D_{3} and D123D_{123} have parity 1+i1+i, ii and 1+i1+i, respectively.

Proof.

We first consider the absolute grading on 𝒜⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z}). By definition, algebra generators corresponding to arcs joining two ends of the same α\alpha arc have grading 11. (See definition 11 of [42] and the equations just preceding it.) In our case, this says that gr⁡ρ12≡gr⁡ρ23≡1\grm\rho_{12}\equiv\grm\rho_{23}\equiv 1. From the relations ρ1⋅ρ23=ρ123\rho_{1}\cdot\rho_{23}=\rho_{123}, ρ1⋅ρ2=ρ12\rho_{1}\cdot\rho_{2}=\rho_{12}, and ρ2⋅ρ3=ρ23\rho_{2}\cdot\rho_{3}=\rho_{23}, we see that gr⁡ρ123≡gr⁡ρ1+1\grm\rho_{123}\equiv\grm\rho_{1}+1, gr⁡ρ2≡gr⁡ρ1+1\grm\rho_{2}\equiv\grm\rho_{1}+1, and gr⁡ρ3≡gr⁡ρ2+1≡gr⁡ρ1\grm\rho_{3}\equiv\grm\rho_{2}+1\equiv\grm\rho_{1}. The statement now follows from the fact that gr∂𝐱≡gr𝐱+1\grm\partial\mathbf{x}\equiv\grm\mathbf{x}+1. ∎

We will also need to know how the DID_{I}’s behave with respect to the Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} grading. Let us write V𝔰0:=H​F​K^​(Kμ,𝔰)V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}:=\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu},\mathfrak{s}), so we have a decomposition V0≃⊕𝔰V0𝔰V^{0}\simeq\oplus_{\mathfrak{s}}V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}, and similarly for V1V^{1}, where the indexing sets in the sums are Spinc​(Y,γμ){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\mu}) and Spinc​(Y,γλ){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\lambda}), as defined in [25]. Elements of Spinc​(Y,γμ){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\mu}) are represented by homology classes of nonvanishing vector fields on YY with fixed behavior on ∂Y\partial Y. (Recall that two nonvanishing vector fields are said to be homologous if they are homotopic on the complement of a ball in YY.) The sets Spinc​(Y,γμ){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\mu}) and Spinc​(Y,γλ){\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\lambda}) are in bijection, but not canonically so, since the boundary conditions are different.

Lemma 3.8.

There is a bijection j:Spinc​(Y,γμ)→Spinc​(Y,γλ)j:{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\mu})\to{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\lambda}) which respects the action of H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y) and for which

D1\displaystyle D_{1} :V𝔰0→Vj⁡(𝔰)1\displaystyle:V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}\to V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})} D2\displaystyle D_{2} :Vj⁡(𝔰)1→V𝔰−λ0\displaystyle:V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})}\to V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}-\lambda} D3\displaystyle D_{3} :V𝔰0→Vj⁡(𝔰)+λ+μ1\displaystyle:V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}\to V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})+\lambda+\mu}
D12\displaystyle D_{12} :V𝔰0→V𝔰−λ0\displaystyle:V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}\to V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}-\lambda} D23\displaystyle D_{23} :Vj⁡(𝔰)1→Vj⁡(𝔰)+μ1\displaystyle:V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})}\to V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})+\mu} D123\displaystyle D_{123} :V𝔰0→Vj⁡(𝔰)+μ1\displaystyle:V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}\to V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})+\mu}

This is essentially Lemma 11.42 of [29], but stated so as to clarify the dependence on μ\mu and λ\lambda.

Proof.

Huang and Ramos [23] have constructed a grading gr{{\mathrm{gr}}} on C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda). This grading lives in a set S⁡(ℋ)S(\mathcal{H}) of homotopy classes of nonvanishing vector fields on YY which satisfy certain boundary conditions. To be specific, for each elementary idempotent ι\iota in the algeba 𝒜⁡(𝒵)\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{Z}), there is an associated vector field vιv_{\iota} on ∂Y\partial Y, and if v∈S⁡(ℋ)v\in S(\mathcal{H}), then v|∂Yv|_{\partial Y} should be equal to vιv_{\iota} for some elementary idempotent ι\iota.

Similarly, Huang and Ramos consider the set G⁡(𝒵)G(\mathcal{Z}) of homotopy classes of nonvanishing vector fields on ∂Y×[0,1]\partial Y\times[0,1], subject to the constraint that v|∂Y×0=vιv|_{\partial Y\times 0}=v_{\iota} and v|∂Y×1=vι′v|_{\partial Y\times 1}=v_{\iota^{\prime}} for some elementary idempotents ι\iota and ι′\iota^{\prime}. They show that G⁡(𝒵)G(\mathcal{Z}) forms a groupoid under concatenation, and that it acts on the grading set S⁡(ℋ)S(\mathcal{H}), again by concatenation. In section 2.3 of [23], they construct explicit vector fields vIv_{I} on ∂Y×[0,1]\partial Y\times[0,1] associated to each ρI\rho_{I}; the grading of ρI​x\rho_{I}x is the vector field vI⋅gr⁡xv_{I}\cdot\grm x, where ⋅\cdot denotes the action by concatenation.

The grading of [23] contains the Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} grading, in the sense that if 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a generator of C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda), then its Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} grading is 𝔰⁡(𝐱)=p⁡(gr⁡𝐱)\mathfrak{s}(\mathbf{x})=p(\grm\mathbf{x}), where pp is the forgetful map which takes a homotopy class of vector fields to its homology class. By Theorem 1.3 of [23], if 𝐱∈C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\mathbf{x}\in\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda), gr∂𝐱=λ−1⋅gr𝐱\grm\partial\mathbf{x}=\lambda^{-1}\cdot\grm\mathbf{x}, where λ\lambda is a vector field on ∂Y×[0,1]\partial Y\times[0,1] which is supported in a ball. It follows that 𝔰⁡(∂𝐱)=𝔰⁡(𝐱)\mathfrak{s}(\partial\mathbf{x})=\mathfrak{s}(\mathbf{x}), and hence that p⁡(vI)⋅𝔰⁡(DI​𝐱)p(v_{I})\cdot\mathfrak{s}(D_{I}\mathbf{x}) = 𝔰⁡(𝐱)\mathfrak{s}(\mathbf{x}).

If 𝔰∈Spinc​(Y,γμ)\mathfrak{s}\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\mu}), we define j⁡(𝔰)=p⁡(v1−1)⋅𝔰j(\mathfrak{s})=p(v_{1}^{-1})\cdot\mathfrak{s}. By construction, D1:V𝔰0→Vj⁡(𝔰)1D_{1}:V^{0}_{\mathfrak{s}}\to V^{1}_{j(\mathfrak{s})}. Similarly, we see that

𝔰⁡(D3​𝐱)=p⁡(v3−1)⋅𝔰⁡(𝐱)=p⁡(v3−1⋅v1)⋅j⁡(𝔰⁡(𝐱)).\mathfrak{s}(D_{3}\mathbf{x})=p(v_{3}^{-1})\cdot\mathfrak{s}(\mathbf{x})=p(v_{3}^{-1}\cdot v_{1})\cdot j(\mathfrak{s}(\mathbf{x})).

The set of homology classes of nonvanishing vector fields on ∂Y×[0,1]\partial Y\times[0,1] which restrict to vι0v_{\iota_{0}} on one end and vι1v_{\iota_{1}} on the other is an affine copy of H1​(∂Y×[0,1])≃H1​(∂Y)H_{1}(\partial Y\times[0,1])\simeq H_{1}(\partial Y). Thus if I1I_{1} is the idempotent of the groupoid G⁡(𝒵)G(\mathcal{Z}) corresponding to the idempotent ι1\iota_{1}, we must have p⁡(v3−1⋅v1)=p⁡(I1)+αp(v_{3}^{-1}\cdot v_{1})=p(I_{1})+\alpha, for some α∈H1​(∂Y)\alpha\in H_{1}(\partial Y). The arguments for the other DID_{I}’s are very similar. ∎

Proposition 3.9.

Suppose that YY is Floer simple, that α∈S​l​(Y)\alpha\in Sl(Y) is a Floer simple filling slope, and that μ,λ∈H1​(∂Y)\mu,\lambda\in H_{1}(\partial Y) satisify μ⋅λ=1\mu\cdot\lambda=1. Then C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) is determined by α\alpha and τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y).

Proof.

It suffices to show that C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) is determined for one particular choice of μ\mu and λ\lambda, since the invariant of any other choice can then be determined using the change of basis bimodules in [30].

The knots KμK_{\mu}, KλK_{\lambda} are Floer simple, so all the elements of V0V_{0} have the same ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading. Similarly, all elements of V1V_{1} have the same ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 grading. By Lemma 3.7, either D2=D123=0D_{2}=D_{123}=0 or D1=D3=0D_{1}=D_{3}=0. Writing C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ+μ)=W0⊕W1\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda+\mu)=W^{0}\oplus W^{1}, we have W1=𝐫⊠V0⊕𝐪⊠V1W^{1}=\mathbf{r}\boxtimes V^{0}\oplus\mathbf{q}\boxtimes V^{1}. Denote by D:W1→W1D:W^{1}\to W^{1} the contribution to ∂\partial coming from provincial differentials; then we have H⁡(W1,D)=H​F​K^​(Kμ+λ)H(W^{1},D)=\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu+\lambda}). By choosing NN sufficiently large, we can ensure that μ+λ=λ0−(N−1)​μ\mu+\lambda=\lambda_{0}-(N-1)\mu is in the interior of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). It follows that H​F​K^​(Kμ+λ)\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu+\lambda}) is Floer simple and has dimension equal to |H1​(Y⁡(μ+λ))|=|H1​(Yλ)|−|H1​(Yμ)|=dimV1−dimV0.|H_{1}(Y(\mu+\lambda))|=|H_{1}(Y_{\lambda})|-|H_{1}(Y_{\mu})|=\dim V_{1}-\dim V_{0}. Referring to the figure, we see that the only contribution to the provincial differential DD comes from the arrow labeled 1⊗ρ31\otimes\rho_{3}. Thus the map ρ3:V0→V1\rho_{3}:V^{0}\to V^{1} is an injection. Similarly, by considering

C​F​D^​(Y,μ+λ,λ)=C​F​D​A^​(τλ−1)⊠C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu+\lambda,\lambda)=\widehat{CFDA}(\tau_{\lambda}^{-1})\boxtimes\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda)

we deduce that the map D1:V0→V1D_{1}:V_{0}\to V_{1} is injective. Since D1D_{1} and D3D_{3} are nontrivial, we must have D2=D123=0D_{2}=D_{123}=0.

Let 𝔰m​a​x∈S⁡[H​F​K^​(Kμ)]\mathfrak{s}_{max}\in S[\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu})] be maximal, in the sense that if 𝔰max+α∈S⁡[H​F​K^​(Kμ)]\mathfrak{s}_{\max}+\alpha\in S[\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu})] (where α∈H1​(Y)\alpha\in H_{1}(Y)), then ϕ⁡(α)≤0\phi(\alpha)\leq 0.

Lemma 3.10.

j⁡(𝔰max)j(\mathfrak{s}_{\max}) is maximal in S​[H​F​K^​(Kλ)]S[\widehat{HFK}(K_{\lambda})].

Proof.

It is well known [35] that H​F​K^\widehat{HFK} detects the Thurston norm, in the sense that if K⊂Y⁡(α)K\subset Y(\alpha), then

max{ϕ(𝔰−𝔰′)|𝔰,𝔰′∈S[H​F​K^(K)]}=∥Y∥+|ϕ(α))|.\max\{\phi(\mathfrak{s}-\mathfrak{s}^{\prime})\,|\,\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{s}^{\prime}\in S[\widehat{HFK}(K)]\}=\|Y\|+|\phi(\alpha))|.

=max{ϕ(𝔰−𝔰′)|𝔰,𝔰′∈S[H​F​K^(Kλ)]}.\displaystyle=\max\{\phi(\mathfrak{s}-\mathfrak{s}^{\prime})\,|\,\mathfrak{s},\mathfrak{s}^{\prime}\in S[\widehat{HFK}(K_{\lambda})]\}.

We represent C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) by a directed graph like that shown in Figure 3, with a vertex for each generator and an edge for each potential component of the differential; that is, for each pair of generators 𝐱,𝐲\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} whose ℤ/2{{\mathbb{Z}}}/2 and Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} gradings are compatible with having DI​𝐱=𝐲D_{I}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y} for some DID_{I}, we draw an edge from 𝐱\mathbf{x} to 𝐲\mathbf{y} and label it with DID_{I}.

Lemma 3.11.

Each vertex of the graph associated to C​F​D^​(Y,μ,λ)\widehat{CFD}(Y,\mu,\lambda) has valence two.

Proof.

First suppose that 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a generator of V0V^{0}. We say 𝔰\mathfrak{s} is occupied if 𝔰∈S​[H​F​K^​(Kμ)]\mathfrak{s}\in S[\widehat{HFK}(K_{\mu})], and unoccupied otherwise; similarly for j⁡(𝔰)∈Spinc​(Y,γλ)j(\mathfrak{s})\in{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}(Y,\gamma_{\lambda}), but with KλK_{\lambda} in place of KμK_{\mu}. The claim is equivalent to saying that if j⁡(𝔰)j(\mathfrak{s}) is occupied, then exactly one of 𝔰\mathfrak{s} and j⁡(𝔰)+μj(\mathfrak{s})+\mu is occupied.

Write j⁡(𝔰)=j⁡(𝔰m​a​x)−αj(\mathfrak{s})=j(\mathfrak{s}_{max})-\alpha for α∈H1​(Y)\alpha\in H_{1}(Y). We consider the situation case by case, depending on the value of ϕ⁡(α)\phi(\alpha).

    0≤ϕ⁡(α)<ϕ⁡(μ)0\leq\phi(\alpha)<\phi(\mu). 4. Intervals of L-space filling slopes

Now that the “proper coloring” condition of Proposition 3.6 is in place, we are equipped to tackle the problem of describing L-space intervals in terms of 𝒟τ​(Y){{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}(Y) and a slope from the interior of the L-space interval. We begin by establishing some conventions.

4.1. Conventions for slopes and homology

If YY is a compact oriented three-manifold with torus boundary, then a slope of YY is a nonseparating, oriented, simple closed curve in ∂Y\partial Y. Such objects correspond bijectively to primitive elements of H1​(∂Y)/{±1}H_{1}(\partial Y)/\{\pm 1\}, or equivalently, to elements of ℙ​(H1​(∂Y)){{\mathbb{P}}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)). Any choice of basis (m,l)(m,l) for H1​(∂Y)H_{1}(\partial Y) specifies homogeneous coordinates nm+n′l↦[n:n′]nm+n^{\prime}l\mapsto[n\!:n^{\prime}] on ℙ​(H1​(∂Y)){{\mathbb{P}}}(H_{1}(\partial Y)), to which we usually refer in terms of the affinization

(1) H1​(∂Y)∖{0}\displaystyle H_{1}(\partial Y)\setminus\{0\} →ℚ∪{∞},\displaystyle\to{{\mathbb{Q}}}\cup\{\infty\},
n​m+n′​l\displaystyle nm+n^{\prime}l ↦n/n′.\displaystyle\mapsto n/n^{\prime}.

Let ι:H1​(∂Y)→H1​(Y)\iota:H_{1}(\partial Y)\to H_{1}(Y) be the map induced by inclusion. We fix a basis (m,l)(m,l) for H1​(∂Y)H_{1}(\partial Y) such that ll is a generator of ker​ι{{\text{ker}\ }}\iota and m⋅l=1m\cdot l=1. The generator ll is the homological longitude of YY; it is well defined up to sign. In contrast, the choice of mm is only well defined up to the addition of a multiple of ll. Consequently, the numerator of π⁡(n​m+n′​l)=n/n′\pi(nm+n^{\prime}l)=n/n^{\prime} is canonical (up to sign), but the denominator depends on the choice of mm.

To Dehn fill YY along a slope μ=n​m+n′​l∈H1​(∂Y)\mu=nm+n^{\prime}l\in H_{1}(\partial Y), one attaches a 2-handle along the simple closed curve associated to μ\mu, and then fills in the remaining S2S^{2} boundary with a 3-ball. The resulting manifold, which we denote by Y⁡(μ)Y(\mu) or Y⁡(n/n′)Y(n/n^{\prime}), has homology H1​(Y⁡(μ))=H1​(Y)/(ι⁡(μ))H_{1}(Y(\mu))=H_{1}(Y)/(\iota(\mu)), which has order |n||n| if H1​(Y)H_{1}(Y) is torsion free.

Any non-zero Dehn filling Y⁡(μl)Y(\mu_{\textsc{l}}) produces a knot Kμl:=core⁡(Y⁡(μl)∖Y)⊂Y⁡(μl)K_{\mu_{\textsc{l}}}:=\mathrm{core}(Y(\mu_{\textsc{l}})\setminus Y)\subset Y(\mu_{\textsc{l}}), on which one can now perform Dehn surgery. We begin by making some simplifying assumptions, without loss of generality.

Suppose that YY is Floer simple, that μl=p​m+q​l\mu_{\textsc{l}}=pm+ql is an L-space slope, and that we wish to determine if μ=n​m+n′​l\mu=nm+n^{\prime}l is an L-space slope for YY. Proof.

Theorem 4.2 already correctly characterizes the cases of β=0\beta=0, corresponding to the Dehn filling Y⁡(μl)Y(\mu_{\textsc{l}}), which we already know to be an L-space, and n=0n=0, for which the filling Y⁡(l)Y(l) is not a rational homology sphere, hence not an L-space. Likewise, we know that any L-space slope μl=p​m+q​l\mu_{\textsc{l}}=pm+ql must have p≠0p\neq 0. Since we are free to replace μl\mu_{\textsc{l}} with −μl-\mu_{\textsc{l}} or μ\mu with −μ-\mu, we may take p,β>0p,\beta>0 without loss. Lastly, by Lemma 3.5, we can approximate μl\mu_{\textsc{l}} with a primitive L-space slope μl′=p′​m+q′​l\mu^{\prime}_{\textsc{l}}=p^{\prime}m+q^{\prime}l (with q′≠0q^{\prime}\neq 0) such that p′​g>deg[m¯]⁡τc​(Y)p^{\prime}g>\deg_{[\bar{m}]}\!{{\tau^{\mathrm{c\mkern-1.5mu}}}}(Y) and gcd⁡(p′​g,β′)=1\gcd(p^{\prime}g,\beta^{\prime})=1, where β′:=μl′⋅μ\beta^{\prime}:=\mu^{\prime}_{\textsc{l}}\cdot\mu. ∎

We henceforth consider the assumptions of Proposition 4.5 to hold. Given such initial data, we have a primary tool from Heegaard Floer homology to determine whether μ\mu is an L-space slope for the Floer simple manifold YY: namely, Proposition 3.6. To exploit this proposition, we must exhibit Y⁡(μ)Y(\mu) as zero surgery on an L-space, given the L-space slope μl\mu_{\textsc{l}} for YY. Fortunately, a standard such construction exists, whereby we first express Y⁡(μ)Y(\mu) as some α/β\alpha/\beta-surgery on Y⁡(μl)Y(\mu_{\textsc{l}}), and then reexpress this as a zero surgery on a connected summed knot inside Y⁡(μl)​#​L​(β,α∗)Y(\mu_{\textsc{l}})\#L(\beta,\alpha^{*}), for some α∗≡−α−1​(mod​β)\alpha^{*}\equiv-\alpha^{-1}\,({{\mathrm{mod\;}}}\beta).

5. Seifert Fibered L-spaces

To illustrate the usage of our new L-space interval tool 𝒟τ{{\mathcal{D}^{\tau\!}}}, in this section we exploit Theorem 4.2 to offer a simple alternative proof of a known result: namely, the classification of Seifert fibered spaces over S2S^{2} which are L-spaces. We restrict to the S2S^{2} case because it is the most interesting one, as no higher genus Seifert fibered spaces are L-spaces, and all oriented Seifert fibered spaces over ℝ​ℙ2{{\mathbb{R}}}{{\mathbb{P}}}^{2} are L-spaces [7].

5.1. Seifert fibered L-spaces, a history

Up until now, the classification of Seifert fibered L-spaces has relied, at least in one direction, on the classification of oriented Seifert fibered spaces MM over S2S^{2} admitting transverse foliations, a problem which dates back at least to 1981, when Eisenbud, Hirsch, and Neumann [11] re-expressed this foliations problem in terms of a criterion on representations of π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) in Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}\!, the universal cover of the group of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of S1S^{1}\mkern-4.5mu.

A few years later, Jankins and Neumann [24] reformulated the criterion of [11] in terms of Poincaré’s “rotation number” invariant on Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}\!, a development which, along with the correct conjecture that this criterion is met in Homeo+~​S1\widetilde{\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}}S^{1}\! if and only if it is met in a smooth Lie subgroup thereof, allowed them to write down an explicit characterization of Seifert fibered manifolds over S2S^{2} admitting transverse foliations. With the exception of one special case, they also showed that this list was complete. It took more than a decade before Naimi [33] resolved this outstanding case using dynamical methods, and more than a decade after that before Calegari and Walker [9] generalized Naimi’s methods to provide a proof of the Jankins-Neumann classification that did not appeal to smooth Lie subgroups.

In the late 1990’s, Eliashberg and Thurston [12] proved that one can associate a weakly symplectically fillable contact structure to any C2C^{2} cooriented taut foliation on a closed three-manifold—a result which Kazez and Roberts [28], and independently Bowden [5], have recently extended to C0C^{0} foliations. Since Ozsváth and Szabó have [38] shown that this contact structure gives rise to a nontrivial class in Heegaard Floer homology, this proves that L-spaces do not admit co-oriented taut foliations.

In the converse direction, Lisca and Matić [31] proved that a Seifert fibered manifold MM over S2S^{2} admits contact structures in each orientation which are transverse to the fibration if and only if MM belongs to the explicit set characterized by Jankins and Neumann. Lisca and Stipsicz then showed [32] that if there is an orientation on a Seifert fibered manifold MM over S2S^{2} for which no positive contact structure is transverse to the fibration, then MM is an L-space.

Since our own answer matches that of Jankins and Neumann, one could take the non-L-space/transverse-foliation equivalence for Seifert fibered manifolds over S2S^{2} as a corollary of Theorem 5.1 below. As for our L-space classification itself, however, the proof no longer requires foliations, dynamical methods, or even (after the proof of Theorem 4.2) contact or symplectic geometry. It only uses ordinary homology and one computation of Turaev torsion from a homology presentation.

6. Gluings along torus boundaries

The introduction to Section 5 discusses how, for Seifert fibered spaces over S2S^{2} (although the same is true for all Seifert fibered spaces [7, 14]), the property of admitting a cooriented taut foliation is equivalent to the property of not being an L-space.

6.1. Equivalent properties for Seifert fibered spaces

In fact, this pair of equivalent properties belongs to a larger list.

Theorem 6.1 ([11, 38, 32, 8]).

Suppose MM is a Seifert fibered space over S2S^{2}. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    MM admits a cooriented taut foliation.

  2. (2.ρ\rho)

    There exists a homomorphism ρ:π1​(M)→Homeo+​ℝ\rho:\pi_{1}(M)\to\mathrm{Homeo}_{+}{{\mathbb{R}}} with non-trivial image.

  3. (2.LO)

    The fundamental group π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) admits a left ordering.

  4. (3)

    MM is not an L-space.

Summary of Proof.

Our idiosyncratic numbering owes to a result of Boyer, Rolfsen, and Wiest [8], which implies that (2.ρ)=(2.LO)(2.\rho)=(2.\mathrm{LO}) for (a superset of) all closed, prime, oriented three-manifolds. We also have (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3) for all closed oriented three-manifolds, as shown by Ozsváth and Szabó in the case of C2C^{2} foliations [38], a result recently extended to C0C^{0} foliations by Kazez and Roberts [28], and independently by Bowden [5].

More is known for Seifert fibered spaces. For Seifert fibrations over S2S^{2}, we have (1)=(2)(1)=(2) as a corollary of a result by Eisenbud, Hirsh, and Neumann [11]. The result that (3)⇒(1)(3)\Rightarrow(1) is due to Lisca, Matić, and Stipsicz for fibrations over S2S^{2} [31, 32], Boyer, Gordon, and Watson for fibrations over ℝ​ℙ2{{\mathbb{R}}}{{\mathbb{P}}}^{2} [7], and Gabai for fibrations with positive first betti number [14]. One could also regard the classification by Jankins, Neumann [24], and Naimi [33] of Seifert fibered spaces over S2S^{2} satisfying (1), together with the classification in the present article’s Theorem 5.1 of Seifert fibered L-spaces over S2S^{2}, as an alternative proof that (1)=(3)(1)=(3). ∎

The above result motivated a conjecture of Boyer, Gordon, and Watson [7] that properties (2) and (3) above are equivalent for all closed, prime, oriented three-manifolds.

6.2. Gluing results

To further explore the relationship of the above properties, Boyer and Clay [6] studied how each of these properties glue together when one splices together Seifert fibered spaces along the toroidal boundaries of fiber complements to form a graph manifold. In the process, Boyer and Clay observed that properties (1) and (2) obey a similar criterion determining when they admit compatible gluings. The property (3) of being a non-L-space proved less tractable for this exercise, but Boyer and Clay conjectured that property (3) should follow a similar gluing pattern to that of (1) and (2).

We are now able to confirm their conjecture in the case in which two Floer simple manifolds glued along their torus boundaries have the interiors of their L-space intervals overlap via the gluing map. In fact, there is no requirement that these Floer simple manifolds be graph manifolds.

7.1. Generalized solid tori

The Seifert fibred spaces Ng=M(∅;1/g,−1/g)N_{g}=M(\emptyset;1/g,-1/g) provide a motivating example of a class of manifolds with ℒ⁡(Ng)=S​l​(Ng)/[l]\mathcal{L}(N_{g})=Sl(N_{g})/[l]. A generalized solid torus is a Floer simple manifold YY with deg⁡Δ¯​(Y)<gY\deg\overline{\Delta}(Y)<g_{Y}.

If YY is such a manifold, Corollary 2.3 implies that ‖Y‖≤gY−2\|Y\|\leq g_{Y}-2. On the other hand, an embedded surface which generates H2​(Y,∂Y)H_{2}(Y,\partial Y) has at least gYg_{Y} boundary components, so a norm-minimizing surface must have genus 00.

Lemma 7.3.

Suppose that YY is a rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}. If p:ℤ⁡[t]→ℤ⁡[t]/(tgY−1)p:{{\mathbb{Z}}}[t]\to{{\mathbb{Z}}}[t]/(t^{g_{Y}}-1) is the projection, then p⁡(Δ¯​(Y))=kY​(1−tgY)/(1−t).p(\overline{\Delta}(Y))=k_{Y}(1-t^{g_{Y}})/(1-t).
