τ¯​(Y​(l))=τ¯​(Y)1−tgY.\overline{\tau}(Y(l))=\frac{\overline{\tau}(Y)}{1-t^{g_{Y}}}.

By [45], Lemma 3.2, we have

τ¯​(Y⁡(l))=tc|H1(Y(l)|(1−t)2+P⁡(t)\overline{\tau}(Y(l))=\frac{t^{c}|H_{1}(Y(l)|}{(1-t)^{2}}+P(t)

Δ¯​(Y)=kY​tc​(1−tgY)1−t+(1−tgY)​(1−t)​P​(t).\overline{\Delta}(Y)=\frac{k_{Y}t^{c}(1-t^{g_{Y}})}{1-t}+(1-t^{g_{Y}})(1-t)P(t).

If YY is a generalized solid torus, Δ¯​(Y)∼kY​(1−tgY)/(1−t)\overline{\Delta}(Y)\sim k_{Y}(1-t^{g_{Y}})/(1-t).

In contrast, τ⁡(Y)\tau(Y) is not determined by the fact that YY is a generalized solid torus, as can be seen by considering the Seifert-fibred spaces M(∅;a/g,−a/g)M(\emptyset;a/g,-a/g).

7.2. NLS Detection

Next, we study the notion of NLS detection introduced by Boyer and Clay in [6]. Suppose that Y1Y_{1} is a rational homology solid torus and that Y2Y_{2} is a semi-primitive generalized solid torus. Given a primitive class α∈H1​(Y1)\alpha\in H_{1}(Y_{1}), choose an orientation reversing homeomorphism φ:∂Y1→∂Y2\varphi:\partial Y_{1}\to\partial Y_{2} with φ∗​(α)=l\varphi_{*}(\alpha)=l, where l∈H1​(∂Y2)l\in H_{1}(\partial Y_{2}) is the homological longitude. Since Y2Y_{2} is a Floer homology solid torus, H​F^​(Yφ){{\widehat{HF}}}(Y_{\varphi}) is well defined, in the sense that any ϕ\phi satisfying φ∗​(α)=l\varphi_{*}(\alpha)=l will give the same result. We say that α\alpha is NLS detected by Y2Y_{2} if YφY_{\varphi} is not an L-space.

If Y1Y_{1} is Floer simple, it follows from Theorem 1.8 that α\alpha is NLS detected by Y2Y_{2} if and only if α\alpha is not in the interior of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). In fact, there is a direct proof of this fact for any Y1Y_{1}.

Proposition 7.9.

The slope α\alpha is NLS detected by Y2Y_{2} if and only if α\alpha is not in the interior of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y).

Proof.

Suppose that α\alpha is not NLS detected by Y2Y_{2}. Then YφiY_{\varphi_{i}} is an L-space for every φi\varphi_{i} with φi∗(α)=l\varphi_{i*}(\alpha)=l. The manifolds YφiY_{\varphi_{i}} are all obtained by Dehn filling a manifold Y′Y^{\prime} which is constructed by identifying ν⁡(α)⊂∂Y1\nu(\alpha)\subset\partial Y_{1} with ν⁡(l)⊂∂Y2\nu(l)\subset\partial Y_{2}, as in the proof of Lemma 2.7. It follows that Y′Y^{\prime} is Floer simple.

Let μ∈H1​(∂Y′)\mu\in H_{1}(\partial Y^{\prime}) be the class which represents the common image of α∈H1​(∂Y1)\alpha\in H_{1}(\partial Y_{1}) and l∈H1​(∂Y2)l\in H_{1}(\partial Y_{2}). The sutured manifold (Y′,γμ)(Y^{\prime},\gamma_{\mu}) contains an essential annulus AA which separates Y1Y_{1} from Y2Y_{2}. The boundary of AA is a pair of curves parallel to μ\mu. We choose the position of the sutures so that one component of ∂A\partial A lies in R+​(γμ)R_{+}(\gamma_{\mu}) and the other component is in R−​(γμ)R_{-}(\gamma_{\mu}). Decomposing (Y′,γμ)(Y^{\prime},\gamma_{\mu}) along AA gives a new sutured manifold which is the disjoint union of (Y1,γα)(Y_{1},\gamma_{\alpha}) and (Y2,γl)(Y_{2},\gamma_{l}). AA is a product annulus, so it follows from Lemma 8.9 of [26] that

S​F​H​(Y′,γμ)=S​F​H​(Y1,γα)⊗S​F​H​(Y2,γl).SFH(Y^{\prime},\gamma_{\mu})=SFH(Y_{1},\gamma_{\alpha})\otimes SFH(Y_{2},\gamma_{l}).

The tensor product respects the decomposition into Spinc{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}} structures in the sense that c(x⊗y)=j1∗(c(x))+j2∗(c(y))c(x\otimes y)=j_{1*}(c(x))+j_{2*}(c(y)), where ji:Yi→Y′j_{i}:Y_{i}\to Y^{\prime} is the inclusion.

To conclude the proof we use the following two lemmas. The first is probably well-known, but we give a proof just in case.

Lemma 7.10.

Suppose YY is an incompressible rational homology S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}, that l∈H1​(∂Y)l\in H_{1}(\partial Y) is the homological longitude, and that m⋅l=1m\cdot l=1. Then

If YY is a generalized solid torus and m∈H1​(∂Y)m\in H_{1}(\partial Y) satisfies ϕ⁡(m)=gY\phi(m)=g_{Y}, then S​F​H​(Y,γm,O)≃ℤkYSFH(Y,\gamma_{m},O)\simeq{{\mathbb{Z}}}^{k_{Y}}.

S​F​H​(Y,γm,O)=H​F​K^​(Km,O)SFH(Y,\gamma_{m},O)=\widehat{HFK}(K_{m},O), where Km⊂Y⁡(m)K_{m}\subset Y(m) is the dual knot. Since YY is a generalized solid torus, the latter group is Floer simple, hence determined by its Euler characteristic. By Lemma 7.3,

ϕ⁡(χ⁡(H​F​K^​(Km)))=kY​(1−tgY)2(1−t)2.\phi(\chi(\widehat{HFK}(K_{m})))=\frac{k_{Y}(1-t^{g_{Y}})^{2}}{(1-t)^{2}}.

Applying the lemmas to Y2Y_{2}, which has kY2=1k_{Y_{2}}=1, we see that S​F​H​(Y2,γl,O)≃H∗​(S1)SFH(Y_{2},\gamma_{l},O)\simeq H_{*}(S^{1}). For Y′Y^{\prime}, suppose that H1​(Y1​(α))=H1​(Y1)/⟨α⟩H_{1}(Y_{1}(\alpha))=H_{1}(Y_{1})/\langle\alpha\rangle has order dd. The torsion subgroup of H1​(Y′)H_{1}(Y^{\prime}) is H1​(Y1)/⟨gY2​α⟩H_{1}(Y_{1})/\langle g_{Y_{2}}\alpha\rangle, so it has order gY2​dg_{Y_{2}}d, Since gY′=gY2g_{Y^{\prime}}=g_{Y_{2}}, we see that kY′=dk_{Y^{\prime}}=d. 7.3. Examples

We conclude by constructing some examples of generalized solid tori. Some of these were previously known to Hanselman and Watson [18] and Vafaee [46]. We start with the following observation.

Corollary 7.12.

If YY is an irreducible, semi-primitive generalized solid torus, then YY is the complement of a closed gYg_{Y}-strand braid in S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2}.

Proof.

The hypotheses imply that Δ⁡(Y)∼(1−tg)/(1−t)\Delta(Y)\sim(1-t^{g})/(1-t) and that H2​(Y,∂Y)H_{2}(Y,\partial Y) is generated by a gYg_{Y}-times punctured sphere. By Corollary 2.3, it follows that YY fibres over S1S^{1} with fibre of genus 00. ∎

By Proposition 7.8, any knot in S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2} with a lens space surgery is a generalized solid torus. Cebanu [10] showed that a knot of this form is a closed braid in S2S^{2}. Examples of such knots were studied by Buck, Baker, and Leucona in [2]. Many (but not all) of them are derived from knots in the solid torus which have solid torus surgeries. These knots were completely classified by Gabai [15] and Berge [3].

To find other examples, we look for braids in S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2} which have L-space surgeries. One criterion for finding such examples is given here. Suppose σ\sigma is an ordinary gg strand braid in D2×ID^{2}\times I. We can close σ\sigma to get a closed braid in S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2}. Dehn filling S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} along S1×pS^{1}\times p gives the ordinary braid closure σ¯⊂S3\overline{\sigma}\subset S^{3}. We can also fill S1×D2S^{1}\times D^{2} along ∂D2\partial D^{2} to get a closed braid in S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2}, which we denote by σ~\widetilde{\sigma}. Let Δ∈B​rg\Delta\in Br_{g} be the full twist on gg-strands.

Proposition 7.13.

Suppose that σ\sigma is a braid with the property that Kn=Δn​σ¯K_{n}=\overline{\Delta^{n}\sigma} is an L-space knot in S3S^{3} for all n≥0n\geq 0. Then the complement of σ~\widetilde{\sigma} is a semi-primitive generalized solid torus.

Proof.

Let L⊂S3L\subset S^{3} be the link which is the union of K=σ¯K=\overline{\sigma} and the braid axis BB. The braid σ~\tilde{\sigma} is the image of KK in the S1×S2S^{1}\times S^{2} obtained by doing 00-surgery on BB.

Let L⁡(a,c)L(a,c) be the manifold obtained by doing aa surgery on KK and cc surgery on AA, where a∈ℤa\in{{\mathbb{Z}}} and c∈ℚc\in{{\mathbb{Q}}}. Then L(a,−1/n)L(a,-1/n) is the result of a+n​g2a+ng^{2} surgery on KnK_{n}. Using Seifert’s algorithm, it is easy to see that there is a constant C⁡(σ)C(\sigma) with the property that g⁡(Kn)≤C⁡(σ)+n​g​(g−1)/2g(K_{n})\leq C(\sigma)+ng(g-1)/2. Thus if a>2​C​(σ)a>2C(\sigma), then a+n​g2≥2​g​(Kn)−1a+ng^{2}\geq 2g(K_{n})-1 for all n≥0n\geq 0. By hypothesis, KnK_{n} is a positive L-space knot, so L(a,−1/n)L(a,-1/n) is an L-space for all n>0n>0.

Now let Y¯\overline{Y} be the manifold obtained by doing aa surgery on KK, and let Y=Y¯−ν⁡(B)Y=\overline{Y}-\nu(B). There is a slope α0∈S​l​(Y)\alpha_{0}\in Sl(Y) so that Y⁡(α0)=L⁡(a,0)Y(\alpha_{0})=L(a,0), and a sequence of slopes α−1/n∈Sl(Y)\alpha_{-1/n}\in Sl(Y) which converge to α0\alpha_{0} such that Y(α−1/n)=L(a,−1/n)Y(\alpha_{-1/n})=L(a,-1/n). It follows that YY is Floer simple and that α0\alpha_{0} is in the closure of ℒ⁡(Y)\mathcal{L}(Y). Since α0\alpha_{0} is not the homological longitude of YY, α0∈ℒ⁡(Y)\alpha_{0}\in\mathcal{L}(Y), so L⁡(a,0)L(a,0) is an L-space. By Proposition 7.8, YY is a generalized solid torus. ∎

We call a closed braid in the solid torus which satisfies the criterion a L-space braid. Examples include:

  • •

    Knots in the solid torus with solid torus surgeries (aka Berge-Gabai knots)

  • •

    The twisted torus knots T⁡(p,k​p±1,2,1)T(p,kp\pm 1;2,1) studied by Vafaee [47]

  • •

    Cables of L-space braids [21]

  • •

    Satellites where the pattern knot is a Berge-Gabai knot and the companion is an L-space braid [22]

We conclude with two remarks. First, we conjecture that every positive one-bridge braid (not just the Berge-Gabai knots) is an L-space braid. Since the knot obtained by applying a full twist to a one-bridge braid is again a one-bridge braid, this is equivalent to showing that the closure of any positive one-bridge braid is an L-space knot in S3S^{3}. Second, in light of the last two items, it would be interesting to know if a satellite where both the pattern and the companion are L-space braids is also an L-space braid.
